Post‑casting, the alloy was hot‑rolled and solution‑annealed at 1700 °C, followed by rapid water quenching to preserve the high‑temperature lattice distortion. Hardness was measured by Vickers indentation on polished cross‑sections; the average Hv increased progressively when the casting temperature was reduced, indicating finer microstructures. During tensile tests, a 0.5‑mm extensometer recorded continuous strain data. Peaks in the stress–strain curve coincided with the onset of micro‑indentation densification, supporting a Tabor‑type proportionality between hardness and yield strength. The higher Vickers hardness at the lower casting temperature corresponded to a yield point shift of several percent strain, suggesting that solid‑solution strengthening from the multi‑component lattice, combined with reduced grain size, governs the observed correlation.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc‐melted ingots of the two refractory high‑entropy alloys, TiCrWMoNbReHf and TiVTa, were prepared under identical conditions (high‑purity elemental pieces, 99.9% purity, melted 10 kW induction coil, repeated melting to homogenize, followed by rapid drop casting into a steel mold). Resulting micrographs revealed that TiCrWMoNbReHf exhibited a markedly finer equiaxed grain structure (sub‑10 µm) compared with TiVTa, which showed coarser grains (~30 µm) and a tendency for columnar growth along the casting direction. The richer elemental spectrum in TiCrWMoNbReHf increases lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening, while the presence of Re and Hf promotes the formation of fine, coherent carbides that act as additional obstacles to dislocation motion. Consequently, tensile tests performed at room temperature indicated a higher ultimate tensile strength and yield strength for TiCrWMoNbReHf, whereas TiVTa displayed lower strength but improved ductility, likely due to its larger grain size and fewer secondary phase precipitates. These observations underscore the critical role of compositional complexity and microstructural refinement in dictating the mechanical response of refractory HEAs.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser additive manufacturing by directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate two refractory high‑entropy alloy (HEA) feedstocks, VTiHfReTaZr and HfTaWZrMoNbV, enabling direct comparison of strain‑rate‑dependent strength behavior. Both systems exhibit dense, fine equiaxed microstructures with a pronounced solid‑solution matrix and minimal porosity, yet their constituent atomic size mismatches and valence electron concentrations differ markedly. The VTiHfReTaZr alloy, containing the light V and the larger Hf, tends toward a lower average lattice distortion, resulting in a more compliant lattice that can accommodate dislocation glide more readily at elevated strain rates; consequently, its flow stress increases moderately with strain rate, indicating a weaker strain‑rate sensitivity. In contrast, the HfTaWZrMoNbV composition harbors a higher degree of size mismatch and a higher valence electron concentration, leading to stronger lattice friction and more pronounced dislocation pile‑up under dynamic loading. Therefore, HfTaWZrMoNbV is expected to display a steeper rise in strength with increasing strain rate, reflecting its higher intrinsic strain‑rate sensitivity relative to VTiHfReTaZr.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties

text: In a study of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VHfCrTi synthesized through high‑energy mechanical alloying and subsequent hot pressing, fatigue crack initiation and propagation were investigated by correlating extensometer‑derived elongation data with microstructural evolution. The as‑compactified microstructure displayed a fine, equiaxed grain population (<5 µm) with a homogeneous distribution of solid‑solution strengthened phases and minimal porosity, which collectively contributed to a pronounced strain‑hardening regime that delayed the onset of microcrack nucleation during cyclic loading. Extensometer curves revealed a plateau in nominal strain corresponding to a stabilized cyclic stress amplitude, suggesting a dominant role of grain boundary sliding in accommodating cyclic deformation before crack nucleation. As fatigue progressed, secondary phases of localized Hf‑rich lamellae served as preferential crack paths, leading to a characteristic reduction in strain rate and eventual rapid crack growth. The measured fatigue lives were thus found to be strongly influenced by grain refinement, the coherency of the solid solution matrix, and the spatial distribution of secondary lamellae, underscoring the importance of controlling processing‑induced microstructural features to enhance fatigue resistance in VHfCrTi alloys.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy VNbZrWMoHf was synthesized by vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization and rapid solidification. During aging at 1300 °C, the microstructure evolves through the formation of Laves‑type (V, Zr, Hf)₂(Nb, Mo, W) intermetallics and minor ordered intermetallics such as V₆W. These secondary phases precipitate along grain boundaries and within the matrix, creating a bimodal distribution of hard, brittle intermetallics and a softer, solid‑solution–strengthened matrix. The precipitate morphology is governed by the lattice mismatch and diffusion kinetics of the constituent elements, leading to a fine, quasi‑equiaxed distribution at high cooling rates. Consequently, the alloy displays enhanced yield strength and hardness due to the impeding of dislocation motion by coherent Laves precipitates, while maintaining a reasonable fracture toughness because the intermetallics remain well dispersed and the matrix retains ductility. These findings underline the importance of controlled precipitation in tailoring the mechanical behavior of VNbZrWMoHf and related refractory high‑entropy systems.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: secondary phase precipitation (Laves phases, intermetallics)

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high‑entropy alloy MoTaTiCrNbZrV was performed in a high‑energy planetary mill for 60 h under argon, using a ball‑to‑powder ratio of 10:1 to promote extensive interdiffusion and achieve a fine, homogeneous nanocrystalline matrix. The resultant powder exhibited an average grain size of ~50 nm, as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy. Hot pressing at 1650 °C under a uniaxial load of 70 MPa for 30 min produced near‑full density compacts (≥ 99 % theoretical). Notch‑toughness tests on Vickers‑notched specimens revealed a pronounced decrease in critical stress intensity factor relative to unnotched samples, indicative of high notch sensitivity typical of BCC‑structured brittle alloys. The small grain size amplifies lattice distortion and solute‑atom scattering, strengthening the material but also concentrating stress at notches. Secondary, Zr‑rich precipitates observed at grain boundaries act as crack‑initiation sites, further reducing fracture toughness. Thus, the processing route yields a dense, high‑strength alloy whose notch sensitivity is governed by nanocrystalline solid solution strengthening, grain boundary precipitation, and inherent BCC brittleness.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing produced dense monolithic samples of the two BCC refractory high‑entropy alloys MoZrCrTi and TiVReHfTaCrNb, allowing direct comparison of notch sensitivity and fracture toughness. In both systems the high lattice distortion and solid‑solution hardening confer a relatively low crack‑tip stress intensity at a given loading, yet the microstructural features governing notch response differ. MoZrCrTi, with a comparatively coarse, equiaxed grain population and fewer secondary precipitates, exhibits a lower fracture toughness and higher notch sensitivity; the grain boundaries act as facile crack‑initiation sites in this brittle composition, and the reduced intergranular cohesion amplifies the stress concentration around a pre‑existing notch. Conversely, TiVReHfTaCrNb demonstrates a finer grain size, a higher volume fraction of coherent nanoscale precipitates, and a more uniform distribution of solid‑solution strengthening, which collectively blunt crack propagation and reduce notch sensitivity. Consequently, the TiVReHfTaCrNb alloy is expected to show a higher fracture toughness relative to MoZrCrTi, reflecting the stronger resistance to crack initiation and propagation in its microstructure.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrCrReNb under a high‑purity argon atmosphere yields a dense, equiatomic microstructure dominated by a body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix with minor intermetallic precipitates of ZrRe and CrNb. The as‑cast alloy exhibits a pronounced susceptibility to environmental embrittlement when exposed to moist air; the formation of ZrO₂ and Cr₂O₃ at grain boundaries generates intergranular crack initiation sites, reducing fracture toughness. In situ hydrogen charging experiments reveal that hydrogen diffuses rapidly along the BCC lattice due to the large atomic radii mismatch among Zr, Cr, Re, and Nb, leading to localized embrittlement at grain boundaries and the formation of brittle hydride-like phases. The alloy’s high lattice distortion enhances solid‑solution strengthening but also promotes hydrogen trapping, which manifests as a reduced elongation at fracture and a shift toward brittle failure modes under cyclic loading. Post‑exposure heat treatments at moderate temperatures partially recover ductility by homogenizing the microstructure and reducing hydrogen trapping sites, yet the overall mechanical performance remains limited by the persistent environmental degradation mechanisms inherent to the Zr‑rich BCC HEA.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects

text: The NbTaZrWCr high‑entropy alloy fabricated by directed energy deposition exhibits a fine, columnar microstructure with a pronounced body‑centered cubic matrix and minor intermetallic precipitates rich in Cr and Zr. Electron backscatter diffraction and transmission electron microscopy reveal that these nano‑scale precipitates are coherently incorporated and spaced at sub‑100‑nm intervals, providing effective obstacles to dislocation motion. High‑temperature tensile testing conducted between 600 °C and 900 °C in a controlled‑argon environment shows a progressive increase in yield and ultimate strengths as the precipitate fraction rises from 3 % to 8 % by volume, while the ductility correspondingly decreases. Hardness measurements correlate strongly with the precipitate volume fraction, indicating that the hardening contribution is dominated by precipitation‑strengthening mechanisms rather than solid‑solution effects or grain refinement. These results demonstrate that tailoring secondary phase content through precise laser scanning strategies can systematically enhance the high‑temperature hardness of NbTaZrWCr without compromising its intrinsic toughness.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: In a typical powder‑metallurgy route, the HfNbTa alloy is blended in equal atomic fractions and consolidated by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at temperatures that preserve a single BCC solid solution. Even with optimized dwell times, residual porosity often remains, especially at grain boundaries where sintering kinetics are limited by the dense packing of refractory oxides. Nanoindentation mapping reveals that regions of higher local hardness and modulus correspond to the continuous BCC matrix, whereas porosity manifests as markedly softer, lower‑modulus sites. These voids act as stress concentrators, reducing the critical stress intensity factor and thereby diminishing fracture toughness. During cyclic loading, the same defects become initiation sites for micro‑cracks; their proximity to the softer pores accelerates crack coalescence, lowering fatigue life. Consequently, controlling porosity—through higher sintering temperatures, longer hold times, or pressure‑assisted sintering—directly improves both toughness and endurance, as evidenced by the correlation between homogeneous hardness maps and extended fatigue lifetimes.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of porosity or processing defects on fracture toughness and fatigue performance
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Laser‑directed energy deposition produces highly supersaturated solid solutions in both ReNbVCrHfW and TiCrTaVWZr, yet their microstructures diverge in the distribution and chemistry of secondary phases, which govern hardness trends. In ReNbVCrHfW, the high‑entropy matrix incorporates Re, Nb, V, Cr, Hf, and W, leading to a modest lattice distortion but also a tendency for the formation of fine Re‑rich carbides and Mo‑like intermetallics during rapid solidification. These nanoscale precipitates act as potent obstacles to dislocation glide, elevating hardness through coherent‑precipitate strengthening. Conversely, TiCrTaVWZr, while also a high‑entropy alloy, exhibits a broader range of element sizes and stronger Ti–Zr affinity, promoting the precipitation of Ti–Zr‑rich intermetallic compounds that tend to be larger and less coherently bonded to the matrix. The coarser, more brittle secondary phases provide less effective barrier strength and can introduce sites for crack initiation, resulting in a comparatively lower hardness relative to ReNbVCrHfW. Thus, the finer, more coherently precipitated secondary phases in ReNbVCrHfW are expected to impart a higher hardness trend in these laser‑additively manufactured systems.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc melting of equiatomic W, Cr, V, Zr, Ti, and Nb was conducted under a purified Ar atmosphere with a water‑cooled copper crucible, yielding a dense ingot that was subsequently drop‑cast onto a preheated steel mold to promote rapid solidification. The resulting microstructure exhibited a predominantly body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix with minor intermetallics, whereas the Ni‑based superalloy counterpart, fabricated via single‑crystal directional solidification, displayed a face‑centered cubic (FCC) γ matrix reinforced by coherent γ′ precipitates. Grain size in the HEA was finer, owing to the high cooling rate, which correlates with increased strength at elevated temperatures through grain boundary strengthening. The lattice distortion inherent to the HEA enhances solid‑solution strengthening, whereas the Ni‑based alloy relies on precipitate‑hardening mechanisms that diminish above ~850 °C. Consequently, the WCrVZrTiNb alloy maintained higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths at temperatures exceeding 1200 °C, with a more gradual loss of hardness compared to the Ni‑based superalloy, indicating superior high‑temperature performance.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: TaHfWReMoNb, synthesized by ball‑millled elemental powders and consolidated through spark plasma sintering (SPS), exhibits a complex interplay between severe lattice distortion and high melting temperatures that governs its recrystallization and grain growth behavior. During SPS, rapid joule heating generates a high temperature gradient and intense pulsed current, promoting dense, defect‑rich microstructures with a fine initial grain size. Upon subsequent annealing, the high entropy configuration lowers the energy barrier for nucleation of new, low‑energy grains, yet the strong solid solution strengthening from the wide range of atomic sizes retards the growth of these recrystallized grains. Consequently, the alloy displays a relatively sluggish grain growth rate compared to binary refractory systems, with the grain boundary mobility being further suppressed by the presence of Re, which segregates to boundaries and pins them. The resulting microstructure retains a sub‑10 µm average grain size even after prolonged high‑temperature exposure, preserving the alloy’s high strength while mitigating excessive softening.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Suction casting of TiWNbZrTa and VTiWCr in an argon‑protected furnace produced dense ingots with negligible porosity, allowing a direct comparison of their intrinsic hardening mechanisms. In TiWNbZrTa, the high lattice distortion arising from the large atomic radius mismatch among Ti, W, Nb, Zr, and Ta generates significant solid‑solution strengthening; this is amplified by the presence of ultrafine β‑phase precipitates that pin dislocations, thereby elevating both hardness and yield strength in a manner consistent with Tabor’s correlation. Conversely, VTiWCr, while also exhibiting pronounced lattice strain, displays a more pronounced body‑centered cubic matrix with a higher density of interstitial V atoms that preferentially occupy interstitial sites, causing a different distribution of strain fields. The resulting dislocation–interstitial interaction leads to a slightly lower hardness compared to TiWNbZrTa, and the yield strength follows this trend, remaining lower but still substantial due to the combined solid‑solution effect and the coarse‑grained microstructure. Overall, TiWNbZrTa is expected to show a marginally higher hardness–yield strength coupling than VTiWCr, driven by its finer precipitate spacing and greater lattice distortion.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)

text: Laser‐directed energy deposition of the refractory high entropy alloy ZrReTiNbWHf produces a dense, fine‑grained microstructure dominated by a single BCC solid solution, yet the alloy contains trace amounts of interstitial oxygen and nitrogen that segregate to grain boundaries during rapid cooling. This segregation creates localized sites of reduced cohesion, making the material susceptible to environmental embrittlement when exposed to moisture or acidic atmospheres. The high lattice distortion inherent to the multi‑principal composition amplifies the sensitivity of the grain boundaries to hydrogen ingress: hydrogen atoms diffuse quickly along the high‑entropy lattice, accumulate at dislocation cores and GBs, and lower the energy barrier for crack nucleation. In contrast, the strong BCC matrix offers a high intrinsic resistance to crack propagation, but the presence of hydrogen‑rich, low‑cohesion zones reduces fracture toughness. Controlling the cooling rate to refine the grain size and post‑processing anneals to reduce interstitial content mitigate these embrittling mechanisms, thereby enhancing the alloy’s resistance to hydrogen‐assisted cracking.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy TaMoHfRe is typically synthesized by mechanical alloying of elemental powders followed by hot pressing to achieve a dense, single‑phase solid solution. Thermodynamic assessment begins with the mixing enthalpy (ΔH_mix), which is computed from the pairwise heats of mixing of the constituent elements; the modestly negative or near‑zero ΔH_mix for Ta–Mo–Hf–Re indicates that the alloy will not readily decompose into intermetallics at the processing temperature. The valence electron concentration (VEC), calculated as the weighted average of the valence electrons of Ta, Mo, Hf, and Re, falls within the range associated with body‑centered cubic (BCC) stability, corroborating the single‑phase BCC microstructure observed by X‑ray diffraction. Both the near‑zero ΔH_mix and the VEC in the BCC window suggest a thermodynamic driving force toward a homogeneous solid solution, which, coupled with the high lattice distortion from the disparate atomic sizes, underpins the strong solid‑solution strengthening expected in this alloy system.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc‑melted NbTaCrZrTiVMo was subsequently drop‑cast into an iron‑free mold and annealed at 1900 °C to homogenize the microstructure. Instrumented indentation performed across a temperature series from 25 °C to 1200 °C revealed a monotonic decrease in hardness that closely tracks the decline in yield strength measured in tensile tests, indicating that the same lattice‑distortion and solid‑solution strengthening mechanisms dominate at all temperatures. The elastic modulus extracted from the unloading curves shows only a modest reduction up to 800 °C, reflecting the high lattice stiffness of the bcc matrix, but a pronounced softening beyond this temperature that coincides with the onset of partial phase separation and the growth of intermetallic precipitates. Consequently, the tensile strength at elevated temperatures drops more rapidly than the elastic modulus, suggesting that creep and thermally activated dislocation climb become limiting factors while the underlying lattice resistance remains relatively robust.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: The laser‑additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfNbCrZrVMoW by directed‑energy deposition yielded a predominantly α‑phase microstructure with equiaxed grains averaging 10–15 µm in the as‑built state. Subsequent hot‑isostatic pressing reduced grain size to ~6 µm, producing a pronounced Hall‑Petch hardening effect observed in extensometer‑controlled tensile tests. During elongation measurement, samples with finer grains displayed a higher initial yield point and steeper hardening slope, indicative of increased grain boundary strengthening. In contrast, specimens retaining coarser grains exhibited earlier onset of necking, suggesting reduced resistance to dislocation motion and a lower intrinsic strength. The correlation between grain refinement and both ultimate tensile strength and Vickers hardness was consistent across multiple specimens, underscoring the dominant role of grain boundary density in dictating the mechanical performance of this multi‑component refractory alloy.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: Powder metallurgy was used to blend elemental Ti, V, W, Mo, Re, Ta, and Cr powders, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1700 °C under 30 MPa for 5 min to achieve near‑full density. The resulting microstructure showed a predominantly body‑centered cubic (bcc) matrix with fine equiaxed grains (<5 µm) and a homogeneous distribution of Re‑rich secondary phases. Elastic modulus measurements performed by resonant ultrasound revealed a progressive increase in Young's modulus when the Re and Ta content was elevated, reflecting stronger metallic bonding and higher valence electron concentration. Conversely, samples with higher Ti and V fractions exhibited lower modulus values due to increased covalent character and lattice distortion. Cyclic loading tests up to 10 % strain amplitude demonstrated that alloys with higher modulus possessed longer fatigue lives, attributed to reduced crack initiation from fewer microstructural defects and higher lattice stiffness, while lower modulus variants displayed premature fatigue failure associated with increased plastic deformation and crack propagation.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high entropy alloy MoNbTiWVRe was carried out in a water‑cooled copper crucible under a 1 bar argon atmosphere. After melting the ingot, a series of compositional adjustments was introduced by varying the Re content from 2 at % to 10 at % while keeping the other elements equimolar. The resultant microstructures, examined by SEM and EDS, revealed a predominantly solid solution of bcc matrix with increasing Re promoting the nucleation of fine MoRe and NbRe intermetallic particles. Hardness testing by Vickers indentation showed a monotonic increase in median hardness as the Re fraction grew, correlating with the higher volume fraction and reduced spacing of these intermetallic second phases. Conversely, the fine‑grained bcc matrix alone exhibited a relatively low baseline hardness, underscoring the critical role of the secondary phases in hardening the alloy. The trend suggests that optimizing Re content can tailor the hardness through controlled secondary phase precipitation.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The laser‑additive‑manufactured refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrTaCr exhibits a body‑centered cubic matrix with minor Zr–Ta–Cr intermetallic precipitates that coarsen slowly at elevated temperatures. Compared with conventional Ni‑based superalloys, the ZrTaCr alloy retains a higher lattice stability because of the large atomic size mismatch among Zr, Ta, and Cr, which reduces dislocation mobility and enhances solid‑solution strength. Grain refinement achieved during rapid solidification suppresses creep activation; fine grains provide a large grain‑boundary area that impedes glide, thereby improving high‑temperature yield and ultimate tensile strengths. The absence of γ′ or γ″ precipitates typical of Ni‑superalloys eliminates the risk of precipitate coarsening, granting the ZrTaCr system superior thermal fatigue resistance over prolonged cycles. However, the lack of a coherent strengthening phase limits the low‑temperature ductility relative to Ni‑based alloys, and the high melting point of Zr and Ta restricts processing window. Overall, ZrTaCr shows directional advantages for sustained service above 900 °C, with stronger high‑temperature mechanical behavior but reduced room‑temperature toughness compared to conventional Ni superalloys.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: In this study, the refractory high‑entropy alloy WMoHfTiZr was fabricated by laser‑directed energy deposition and subjected to systematic micro‑ and macro‑structural characterization. Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy revealed a pronounced reduction in elastic modulus relative to the bulk powder feedstock, attributed to the incorporation of sub‑micron porosity and interfacial voids generated during rapid solidification. Quantitative image analysis indicated that porosity levels exceeding 3 vol.% correlated with a marked decrease in fracture toughness, as evidenced by a shift from transgranular to intergranular failure modes and increased crack‑tip opening displacements. Fatigue testing at cyclic stresses approaching the nominal yield strength further underscored the detrimental influence of these processing defects: crack initiation predominantly occurred at pore sites, and the fatigue life shortened by an order of magnitude compared to defect‑free cast counterparts. These findings underscore the necessity of optimizing laser scan strategies and post‑processing densification to mitigate porosity and preserve the intrinsic toughness and fatigue resistance of WMoHfTiZr alloys.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the effect of porosity or processing defects on fracture toughness and fatigue performance

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy V₆₀W₃₀Zr₁₀, fabricated by vacuum induction melting, crystallizes predominantly as a body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with minor Zr‑rich secondary phases at grain boundaries. In this BCC system, the lattice distortion introduced by the large atomic size mismatch between V, W, and Zr enhances solid‑solution strengthening but also promotes localized stress concentrations at micro‑notches. Notch sensitivity, defined as the ratio of the nominal stress to the applied stress needed to initiate crack propagation, increases when the fracture toughness is dominated by cleavage along the (100) planes characteristic of BCC crystals. The presence of a fine, homogenous grain structure reduces the effective notch size by redistributing stress, thereby mitigating the severity of stress concentration at a given crack tip. Conversely, coarse grains or segregated Zr‑rich pockets concentrate strain and lower the fracture energy, leading to higher notch sensitivity. Thus, for this brittle BCC HEA, optimizing grain refinement and suppressing secondary phase segregation during casting or thermomechanical processing directly improves fracture toughness by diminishing notch‑induced crack initiation and propagation.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: In the present work a refractory high‑entropy alloy (NbWCrTiRe) was fabricated by suction casting under a high‑purity argon atmosphere to minimize oxidation and nitrogen incorporation. A pre‑alloyed master ingot of the stoichiometric composition was melted in an induction furnace, then rapidly transferred into a copper‑cooled mold; the resulting cast retained a coarse, equiaxed microstructure with an average grain size of ~50 µm. Optical microscopy and SEM revealed a homogeneously distributed solid solution of all five elements without detectable secondary phases. Hardness measurements performed with a Vickers indenter at 0.5 kgf loads yielded values ranging from 350 to 380 HV, depending on local microstructural refinement. Corresponding uniaxial tensile tests exhibited yield strengths that closely tracked the Vickers hardness via the Tabor relationship (σ_y ≈ 3 × HV), confirming that the observed hardness is a reliable indicator of the alloy’s resistance to plastic deformation. The modest hardness spread aligns with the expected lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening inherent to the NbWCrTiRe system, while the absence of brittle precipitates ensures a uniform yield response across the cast section.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: MoHfZrVCrNbW was fabricated by ball‑milling of elemental powders followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1900 °C under 40 MPa, achieving dense bulk specimens with <0.5 vol % porosity. X‑ray diffraction revealed a dominant body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix interspersed with minor hexagonal close‑packed (HCP) secondary phases enriched in Hf and Zr. Optical and SEM micrographs show an average grain size of ~15 µm and a high fraction of low‑angle grain boundaries, indicative of effective grain growth control during SPS. Fracture toughness tests performed at room temperature indicated a relatively high K_IC compared to conventional BCC alloys of similar composition. The enhanced toughness is attributed to the fine intergranular network of HCP phases which impede crack initiation by deflecting the crack along the BCC–HCP interfaces, while the abundance of low‑angle grain boundaries promotes plastic accommodation through dislocation glide and grain boundary sliding. Consequently, the combination of solid‑solution strengthening from the high lattice distortion, phase‑induced crack deflection, and low‑angle boundary architecture produces a fracture resistance that increases with the proportion of coherent HCP precipitates and decreases when porosity or high‑angle boundaries become prevalent.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark‑plasma sintering produced a dense ReHfZrTiTaCr alloy in which the primary body‑centred cubic lattice is interrupted by nanoscale Re‑rich precipitates distributed coherently within the matrix. Microhardness measurements reveal a pronounced increase relative to the single‑phase baseline, and this hardening correlates with the volume fraction of the Re‑rich phase: finer, more uniformly spaced precipitates yield a higher hardness, whereas coarsening or agglomeration leads to a slight decline. Tensile testing with extensometer monitoring shows that samples with the highest precipitate density maintain substantial elongation before fracture, suggesting that the coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion without introducing significant brittleness. When the precipitate size grows beyond the critical spacing for coherent strengthening, the alloy exhibits reduced plastic strain and a more pronounced brittle response, highlighting the delicate balance between hardening and ductility governed by secondary phase morphology.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: Powder‑metallurgy fabrication and spark plasma sintering of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbZrMoVTa yield a dense body with a fine equiaxed γ‑phase lattice and residual porosity below 0.5 %. Subsequent annealing at 1800 °C for 12 h in an inert atmosphere promotes extensive homogenization of the constituent elements and the dissolution of minor secondary intermetallics that were initially present as nanosized precipitates. The elevated temperature reduces lattice distortion by allowing atomic redistribution, thereby decreasing the magnitude of solid‑solution strengthening but simultaneously refining the grain size to ~2 µm due to recovery and recrystallization. Microhardness measurements indicate that the homogenized microstructure exhibits a modest reduction in hardness compared to the as‑sintered state, yet the uniform distribution of alloying elements enhances tensile ductility by mitigating localized strain concentrations. Overall, the annealing step improves compositional uniformity and grain refinement, which together modulate the balance between strength and plasticity in this NbZrMoVTa high‑entropy system.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: The refractory high entropy alloy TiVCrTa, synthesized by laser additive manufacturing through directed energy deposition, demonstrates a pronounced tendency toward high‑temperature structural stability driven by thermodynamic factors. Calculated mixing enthalpies for the equiatomic composition are negative, indicating an energetically favorable solid solution formation that suppresses intermetallic precipitation during rapid solidification. Valence electron concentration (VEC) is computed to be approximately 5.6, placing the alloy firmly in the body‑centered cubic (BCC) regime, which correlates with a dense, low‑stacking‑fault energy lattice. The substantial atomic size mismatch among Ti, V, Cr, and Ta generates significant lattice distortion, further enhancing solid solution strengthening without compromising phase homogeneity. Thermodynamic assessments reveal a low Gibbs free energy of mixing across the deposition temperature window, which explains the retention of a single BCC phase and the absence of deleterious secondary phases. Consequently, the alloy’s microstructure is expected to exhibit fine equiaxed grains and minimal porosity, factors that collectively contribute to its predicted superior high‑temperature strength and ductility.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: Arc‐melting of the equiatomic precursor of CrHfMoReTiTaV was performed under a high‑purity Ar atmosphere, with each melt remelted five times to ensure homogeneity; subsequent drop casting onto a copper hearth produced a cylindrical ingot that was then sectioned into tensile specimens oriented parallel and perpendicular to the casting direction. Standard ASTM E8 tensile testing was carried out on both orientations at room temperature. Samples cut parallel to the casting direction exhibited a pronounced yield plateau followed by higher ultimate tensile stress and greater strain‑to‑failure compared to the perpendicular specimens, indicating significant anisotropy. Optical and SEM analyses revealed that the parallel orientation preserved a columnar grain morphology aligned along the casting axis, resulting in more coherent grain boundaries and reduced grain‑boundary sliding. In contrast, the perpendicular samples contained a more equiaxed grain structure and a higher density of intergranular pores, both of which facilitated earlier plastic localization and reduced ductility. These observations underscore the role of texture‐induced grain alignment in tailoring the anisotropic tensile response of this refractory HEA.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In a series of laser‑directed‑energy‑deposition builds, MoReZrCrTi coupons were fabricated from a pre‑alloyed powder (99.5 % purity) by scanning a 10 W Nd:YAG laser at 200 mm s⁻¹ with a 0.8 mm beam diameter, layer thickness 50 µm, and hatch spacing 0.4 mm. Post‑processing involved water‑jet polishing to remove melt‑pool irregularities, followed by a vacuum anneal at 1650 °C for 4 h to homogenize the microstructure. Tensile testing at strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹ revealed a pronounced strain‑rate‑dependent hardening: the flow stress increased markedly at higher rates, a trend attributed to the suppression of dislocation glide by the high lattice distortion inherent to the Mo–Re–Zr–Cr–Ti system and the concomitant increase in solid‑solution strengthening. Grain sizes measured by EBSD (≈3–5 µm) remained stable across rates, indicating that the rate sensitivity arises mainly from enhanced short‑range order and sluggish diffusion of Re and Zr at elevated strain rates, rather than microstructural evolution.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In a comparative assessment of the refractory high‑entropy alloys HfTiWZrTa and HfTiReVW fabricated by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, the observed trends in elongation at fracture are governed by distinct microstructural attributes. The HfTiWZrTa alloy displays a relatively homogeneous equiaxed grain population with average grain sizes in the sub‑10‑µm range, and its solid‑solution matrix is characterized by moderate lattice distortion due to the size mismatch among Hf, Ti, W, Zr, and Ta. This microstructure supports a uniform distribution of dislocations and facilitates cross‑slip, leading to an extended plastic zone ahead of the crack tip and, consequently, a higher elongation at fracture. In contrast, HfTiReVW contains a pronounced network of secondary carbides and vanadium‑rich intermetallic precipitates that form during solidification; these coherent inclusions act as stress concentrators and impede dislocation mobility, thereby limiting strain hardening and reducing ductility. Although both alloys maintain high strength, the presence of Re and V in HfTiReVW enhances lattice distortion but simultaneously introduces brittle intermetallic phases, which collectively suppress the elongation at fracture relative to HfTiWZrTa.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Suction casting of the NbWMo refractory high‑entropy alloy in an argon‑purged environment produces dense, columnar microstructures with fine equiaxed grains at the surface. Instrumented indentation reveals a hardness plateau at room temperature that rises gradually with depth, reflecting the increased contribution of dislocation storage to the local work hardening. The elastic modulus extracted from the initial elastic recovery shows a modest increase from ~310 GPa at ambient conditions to ~335 GPa at 800 °C, indicative of limited lattice parameter expansion due to the high‑temperature stabilization of the BCC phase. Tensile testing across a temperature range of 25–800 °C demonstrates a pronounced decline in both ultimate tensile strength and yield strength, with the yield point exhibiting a more rapid drop, consistent with the activation of thermally assisted cross‑slip and dislocation climb. The indentation‑derived hardness follows a similar temperature trend, decreasing in step with the tensile strength, thereby confirming that the bulk strength is governed by the same solid‑solution and lattice‑distortion mechanisms that dominate the local mechanical response.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaMoZrTiWV produces a dense, single‑phase body‑centered cubic solid solution that is highly susceptible to texture formation during subsequent rapid solidification or additive manufacturing. When specimens are fabricated by layer‑by‑layer deposition, the directional cooling rate aligns the <111> crystallographic axes along the build direction, establishing pronounced anisotropy in tensile response at high temperature. In a controlled‑atmosphere furnace, tensile tests reveal that samples loaded parallel to the build axis exhibit higher yield strength and lower ultimate strain than those loaded perpendicular to it, reflecting the easier slip of {111}<110> planes in the textured orientation. The anisotropy is further amplified by the differential evolution of vacancy‑driven diffusion: along the build direction, grain boundaries remain more coherently oriented, reducing strain‑rate sensitivity, whereas transverse specimens experience greater grain boundary sliding, leading to earlier onset of plastic instability. This directional dependence underscores the importance of controlling solidification directionality and post‑processing heat treatments to tailor mechanical performance in TaMoZrTiWV.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: In a powder‑metallurgy study of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WReCrVZr processed by spark plasma sintering, the hardness distribution was found to vary systematically with the relative atomic fractions of the constituent elements. Samples with a higher proportion of tungsten and rhenium exhibited markedly higher Vickers hardness, a consequence of the dense packing of these early‑transition metals and the concomitant strengthening of the solid solution through large lattice distortions. As the chromium and vanadium content increased, secondary γ‑Cr₂V‑type intermetallics were observed to precipitate at grain boundaries, reducing the overall hardness relative to the baseline WRe‑rich composition. Conversely, alloys with a higher zirconium fraction displayed a fine network of Zr‑rich σ‑phase precipitates, which, despite contributing to hardness, also introduced porosity during sintering that partially offset the strengthening effect. Thus, hardness peaks in the WRe‑rich regime, diminishes as secondary phases nucleate with increasing Cr or V, and can be partially restored by careful control of Zr‑related precipitation and densification.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In a laser‑additive‑manufactured specimen of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrTiW, the notch sensitivity is governed by the intrinsic brittleness of its body‑centered cubic lattice and by the microstructural evolution during rapid solidification. Three‑point bend fracture‑toughness tests conducted under ASTM E399/E1820 reveal a pronounced dependence of the critical stress intensity factor on the notch root radius: specimens with sharper notches exhibit markedly lower \(K_{IC}\) values, reflecting higher local stress concentrations that accelerate crack initiation. This behaviour can be attributed to the limited capacity of the BCC matrix to accommodate plastic deformation; the lattice distortion introduced by the equiatomic mixture of Zr, Ti, and W generates a high density of coherently pinned dislocations, but the rapid cooling of the directed energy deposition process suppresses grain growth and promotes a fine, nearly single‑phase microstructure. Consequently, the crack propagates with minimal plastic shielding, and notch sensitivity is exacerbated by the small grain size and the absence of secondary ductile phases. Thus, in brittle BCC HEAs such as ZrTiW, enhancing fracture toughness requires either increasing the notch radius, introducing ductile secondary phases, or refining the solid‑state heat‑treatment schedule to broaden grain size and facilitate localized plasticity.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: A stoichiometric mixture of Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W, Re, and V powders (≥99.9 % purity) was pre‑ground to 30 µm, then subjected to high‑energy ball milling in a tungsten carbide vial for 72 h at 500 rpm, achieving a near‑single‑phase solid solution with average crystallite size below 10 nm. During milling, the large atomic radius disparity between Nb/Ta (≈146 pm) and Re/V (≈135–133 pm) introduced significant lattice distortion, evidenced by continuous peak broadening in the X‑ray diffraction pattern and an increased full width at half maximum in the (110) reflection. Subsequent hot‑pressing at 1800 °C under 50 MPa for 10 min consolidated the powder to >99 % relative density, preserving the nanocrystalline texture. Transmission electron microscopy revealed a homogeneous distribution of solute atoms and a low density of coherent secondary phases, confirming that the pronounced lattice strain dominates the strengthening mechanism over any precipitate hardening. The pronounced lattice distortion is expected to impede dislocation motion, thereby enhancing the alloy’s yield strength while maintaining good ductility due to the retained nanoscale grain structure.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc‑melting of TiZrReHf followed by drop casting produced cast ingots with a predominantly solid solution matrix and a distribution of TiZr intermetallic precipitates that varied with alloy composition. Samples with a higher proportion of the refractory element Re displayed a finer dispersion of these intermetallics, which contributed to a noticeably higher hardness relative to Ti‑rich compositions. The increased lattice distortion introduced by Re substitution also impeded dislocation motion, further elevating hardness. In contrast, Ti‑rich alloys exhibited a coarser secondary phase network and lower overall hardness, as the intermetallic precipitates were larger and less effective at blocking slip. Variations in Zr content modulated the size and connectivity of the secondary phase; modest increases in Zr led to a more interconnected intermetallic network, which slightly reduced hardness due to the enhanced ease of crack propagation along these pathways. Overall, the data demonstrate that maximizing the content of Re and maintaining a fine, evenly distributed TiZr secondary phase are key to achieving superior hardness in TiZrReHf cast alloys.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: The powder‑metallurgy route combined with spark plasma sintering produced a fully dense ZrVWReHfMoTi microstructure dominated by a single BCC phase with minor intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries. Three‑point bend fracture toughness tests under ASTM E399/E1820 conditions revealed a marked decrease in fracture toughness with increasing test temperature, indicating thermal softening of the matrix. Correspondingly, tensile tests performed on specimens extracted from the same batch showed a pronounced drop in both ultimate and yield tensile strength as temperature rose from room temperature to 900 °C. The decline in yield strength follows the expected weakening of solid‑solution and lattice‑distortion hardening mechanisms at elevated temperatures, while the reduction in ultimate strength is amplified by the growth of intergranular precipitates that coarsen and act as initiation sites for ductile fracture. The data suggest that the high entropy effect remains effective at room temperature but becomes progressively less influential as thermal activation facilitates dislocation motion and precipitate dissolution.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: The NbCrReTaV refractory high‑entropy alloy produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and subsequent hot‑pressing exhibits a pronounced dependence of yield strength on the degree of solid‑solution strengthening intrinsic to its multi‑principal composition. During alloying, the extensive lattice distortion generated by the size and valence mismatch among Nb, Cr, Re, Ta, and V atoms promotes strong dislocation–solute interactions, thereby elevating the resistance to initial plastic deformation. Hot‑press consolidation further refines the microstructure, yielding a fine equiaxed grain population that synergistically enhances yield strength through grain‑size strengthening, while the retained solid‑solution matrix maintains a high degree of coherency across the grain boundaries. Consequently, the material demonstrates a high yield strength that escalates with increased processing energy, which augments both solute atom distribution and grain refinement, and diminishes porosity, illustrating the critical role of solid‑solution strengthening mechanisms in governing the mechanical performance of this refractory HEA.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: Powders of the refractory high‑entropy alloy MoReTiTa were blended under argon atmosphere to achieve a nominal equiatomic composition, followed by high‑energy ball milling for 48 h to promote solid‑solution homogenization. The milled powders were pressed into cylindrical pellets (Ø 10 mm) under 300 MPa and subjected to spark plasma sintering at 2100 °C for 5 min under a 50 MPa uniaxial load with a 15 V pulsed current. Optical micrographs of the as‑sintered cross‑sections revealed a dense microstructure with a mean grain size of 8–10 µm; electron backscatter diffraction indicated a near‑random orientation distribution. High‑resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy highlighted fine dendritic networks at the grain boundaries, with a typical width of 0.5–1 µm, where the Re concentration was slightly enriched relative to the matrix. Energy‑dispersive spectroscopy confirmed that the dendritic regions possessed a modest compositional deviation (≈+5 at %) from the nominal equiatomic ratio, while the primary matrix remained near‑stoichiometric. The dendrite‑matrix contrast, coupled with the relatively small grain size, suggests that solid‑solution strengthening dominates the mechanical response, whereas the residual segregation may serve as potential sites for crack initiation under high‑temperature loading.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Refractory high‑entropy alloy WHfZr, synthesized by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering, exhibits an elastic modulus that increases systematically with the relative proportion of early transition metals (W, Hf) compared to the late transition metal Zr. This trend reflects the underlying bonding character: W and Hf contribute stronger metallic d‑bonding and higher valence electron concentrations, leading to stiffer lattice frameworks, whereas Zr introduces more metallic‑like s‑p bonding that softens the crystal lattice. Compression tests reveal that compositions enriched in W and Hf reach higher yield stresses before the onset of ductile flow, yet the yield point remains sharp and brittle, characteristic of limited dislocation mobility in these stiff lattices. The measured Young’s modulus scales with the average cohesive energy of the constituent elements, underscoring the pivotal role of electronic structure in governing the elastic response of WHfZr alloys.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering produced a dense VHfNbTaCrW alloy with a body‑centered cubic lattice and an average grain size of approximately 4 µm. The wide variance in atomic sizes among V, Hf, Nb, Ta, Cr, and W leads to pronounced lattice distortion, which dominates the solid‑solution strengthening mechanism. As the solid solution content increases, the interaction between solute atoms and mobile dislocations is enhanced, raising the yield stress. Experimental observations show that the alloy with the highest Hf content exhibits the largest yield strength, consistent with the larger atomic radius of Hf contributing to greater lattice strain. Conversely, samples with higher V or Cr fractions display reduced yield stress, indicating that the smaller atomic radii of these elements diminish the overall lattice distortion. Thus, the yield strength trends in VHfNbTaCrW are governed by the balance of atomic size mismatches and the resulting dislocation‑solute interaction strength.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TiZrWCr produced a single‑phase solid solution that retains a body‑centered cubic (BCC) lattice over the entire compositional range studied. X‑ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy confirm that the lattice parameter expands monotonically with increasing Ti content, reflecting the larger atomic radius of Ti relative to the other constituents. High‑resolution electron backscatter diffraction shows that the as‑cast microstructure consists of equiaxed grains with an average size of 20 µm, and the absence of secondary intermetallics indicates that solid‑solution strengthening dominates the phase stability. The substantial lattice distortion, arising from the five‑element mixture and the size mismatch among Ti, Zr, W, and Cr, suppresses the formation of brittle ordered phases and stabilizes the BCC matrix down to cryogenic temperatures. Thermal analysis reveals that the alloy exhibits a high solidus temperature, corroborating the robustness of the solid solution against phase separation during thermal cycling.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: Vacuum induction melting of TiHfRe produced a fully dense ingot with a single BCC‑like solid solution. Subsequent annealing at 1400 °C for 12 h in an argon‑purged furnace markedly refined the microstructure. X‑ray diffraction indicated a slight contraction of the lattice parameter relative to the as‑cast state, reflecting reduced compositional heterogeneity after homogenization. Optical and SEM imaging revealed a dramatic reduction of Ti‑rich lamellae that were present as precipitates in the cast material. Grain size increased modestly from 15 µm to ~35 µm, yet the internal strain fields were significantly relieved, producing a more uniform stress distribution. The homogenization also suppressed the formation of Re‑rich secondary phases that had previously acted as weak points. Overall, the annealed alloy exhibits a more homogeneous lattice distortion, leading to enhanced strength and fracture toughness by mitigating localized deformation sites.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: In our powder‑metallurgy study, VWHfTiCrMoTa and TiVHfZrMo were fabricated from high‑purity elemental powders and consolidated by spark plasma sintering at 2100 °C under 50 MPa. The sintered compacts were machined into standardized cylinders and subjected to uniaxial compression at room temperature. Both alloys exhibited pronounced asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield responses, a common feature of refractory high‑entropy systems. The VWHfTiCrMoTa alloy, containing a higher proportion of early transition metals, displayed a more pronounced grain‑boundary strengthening effect, leading to a modestly higher compressive yield strength relative to its tensile counterpart. Conversely, TiVHfZrMo, with its substantial Zr content, formed finer equiaxed grains and a more homogeneous solid solution, which resulted in a relatively lower compressive yield strength but a reduced tensile‑to‑compressive yield ratio. The observed trends are consistent with the larger lattice distortion and higher solid‑solution strength in VWHfTiCrMoTa, which favors compressive load resistance, whereas the TiVHfZrMo alloy’s finer microstructure and lower lattice distortion yield a more symmetric yet lower overall yield response.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders (Ta, Ti, V, Zr, Nb, Hf, W) was carried out for 30 h at 600 rpm, producing a nanocrystalline precursor with an average grain size below 100 nm. The milled powder was consolidated by hot pressing at 1650 °C under 50 MPa for 10 min, resulting in fully dense bulk samples. Subsequent additive manufacturing via selective laser melting produced specimens with pronounced columnar grains aligned along the build direction. Tensile testing on the as‑fabricated samples revealed a marked anisotropy: the modulus and ultimate tensile strength were higher when the loading axis coincided with the build direction, while the transverse response exhibited reduced stiffness and lower strength, consistent with the texture-induced alignment of high‑angle grain boundaries. The directional dependence can be attributed to the preferential orientation of the bcc lattice and the distribution of interstitially trapped V and Zr, which strengthen the lattice along the build axis. In contrast, the transverse loading path intersects a higher density of incoherently oriented grain boundaries, leading to enhanced slip activation and lower resistance. Thus, the mechanical alloying and hot‑pressing route combined with additive manufacturing generates a textured microstructure that directly governs anisotropic tensile behavior in the TaTiVZrNbHfW high‑entropy alloy.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The vacuum induction melted VTaTiCrHf alloy exhibited notable ductility at room temperature, with elongation at fracture exceeding typical values for equiatomic refractory high‑entropy systems. This enhanced plasticity originates from a predominantly body‑centered cubic (bcc) matrix refined to sub‑10 µm grains during rapid solidification, which promotes dislocation motion and delays early localization. The high lattice distortion introduced by the five‐element mixture provides effective solid‑solution strengthening, yet the coherent intermetallic precipitates of the V–Cr–Ti system remain sparse and uniformly distributed, thus avoiding premature crack initiation. Moreover, the low interfacial energy between the bcc matrix and the minor Cr‑rich second phases reduces void nucleation under tensile loading. However, any residual porosity introduced during melting or casting limits ductility by acting as stress concentrators; thus careful control of cooling rate and degassing is critical to preserve the observed elongation.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: The compressive yield response of refractory high‑entropy alloys processed by mechanical alloying and hot‑pressing reflects the balance between lattice distortion, solid‑solution strengthening, and defect accommodation under load. In CrWMoV HfTa, the large atomic size mismatch among Cr, W, Mo, V, Hf, and Ta promotes a high degree of lattice distortion, which effectively impedes dislocation motion under compression. Additionally, the mechanical alloying step introduces high densities of sub‑micron grains and high‑angle grain boundaries, providing abundant obstacle sites for slip, while hot‑pressing refines the microstructure and eliminates porosity. This combination typically yields a compressive yield stress that is higher than the tensile yield stress, creating pronounced asymmetry. Conversely, ReCrMoTiV contains a relatively smaller size mismatch and a higher fraction of Re, which has a lower modulus and contributes to a more isotropic stress‑state response. Its grain structure, though also fine, exhibits less severe solid‑solution strengthening, so the compressive yield stress is expected to be closer to the tensile value and overall lower than in CrWMoVHfTa. Thus, CrWMoVHfTa would plausibly display a higher compressive yield trend with greater asymmetry relative to ReCrMoTiV.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: High‑entropy alloy ReHfVTaZrMoNb was fabricated by melting a stoichiometric mixture of high‑purity elemental powders in a vacuum induction furnace at 2500 °C, followed by rapid cooling to suppress segregation and preserve a single solid solution. Optical metallography revealed a bimodal grain structure: a coarse network of equiaxed grains (≈50 µm) interspersed with a fine lamellar phase (≈2 µm). Nanoindentation maps across polished cross‑sections showed that the coarse grains exhibited a relatively uniform hardness of 8–9 GPa and reduced elastic modulus (~250 GPa), whereas the fine lamellae displayed increased hardness (10–12 GPa) and higher modulus (~270 GPa). Tensile testing at room temperature indicated that samples dominated by the fine lamellar network produced higher ultimate tensile strength and yield strength than those with a coarse grain matrix, while elongation at fracture decreased correspondingly. These trends can be attributed to enhanced solid solution strengthening and lattice distortion in the Re‑rich lamellar phase, as well as reduced grain boundary area, which impede dislocation motion. The spatial correlation between local mechanical properties and microstructural features underscores the importance of controlling grain size and phase distribution to optimize the strength–ductility balance in this refractory HEA.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting TaWNbHfTi under a controlled argon atmosphere produces a dense ingot with a predominantly body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix. Microstructural analysis shows that increasing the Hf or Ti content, while keeping Ta and W constant, promotes the precipitation of Hf‑rich B2 and Ti‑rich Laves‑type secondary phases. These intermetallic inclusions act as obstacles to dislocation motion, resulting in a marked rise in microhardness when their volume fraction exceeds a critical threshold. Conversely, compositions that suppress the formation of such secondary phases—by slightly favoring Ta and W—display lower hardness values, attributable to a more coherent solid solution and reduced lattice distortion. The hardness trend thus follows a clear qualitative correlation: higher secondary phase content, especially coherent B2 and Laves structures, correlates with increased hardness due to enhanced Orowan bypass and strain‑age mechanisms, whereas a more homogenous BCC solid solution yields comparatively softer behavior.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: Laser additive manufacturing of refractory high entropy alloys such as NbVCr and HfTiCrV produces rapidly solidified microstructures where the distribution and volume fraction of secondary intermetallic phases play a pivotal role in determining hardness. In NbVCr, the high V content promotes the formation of a coarse, brittle Nb–V–Cr intermetallic network that occupies a substantial fraction of the solidified matrix; this network, while providing load‑bearing strength, also introduces lattice distortion and impedes dislocation motion, leading to a comparatively higher hardness. In contrast, HfTiCrV tends to form a more finely dispersed mixture of Hf–Ti–Cr solid solution and a lower‑volume fraction of secondary Hf–Cr intermetallics, owing to the lower atomic size mismatch between Hf and Ti compared to the Nb–V pair. The finer secondary phase distribution in HfTiCrV results in a lower overall hardening effect, yielding a softer response relative to NbVCr. Thus, qualitatively, NbVCr would be expected to exhibit a higher hardness trend than HfTiCrV, driven mainly by its larger, more continuous secondary phase network.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc‐melting and subsequent drop casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WVZrMoTa produced a nearly single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix with a minor, finely dispersed WC intergranular phase. Post‑solidification homogenization at 1850 °C for 12 h in a tube furnace reduced the residual compositional segregation and dissolved the WC clusters, yielding a more uniform elemental distribution and a slightly coarser, equiaxed grain structure. The homogenized microstructure displayed reduced lattice strain, as confirmed by X‑ray diffraction peak narrowing, and a pronounced decrease in the internal porosity measured by micro‑CT. Scanning electron microscopy revealed that the refined grain boundaries were cleaner and less prone to intergranular cracking. Consequently, the annealed alloy exhibited a higher yield strength and ultimate tensile strength, attributable to the elimination of stress concentrators, while the ductility was modestly improved due to the more homogeneous solid‑solution strengthening and reduced brittle secondary phase content. Overall, homogenization enhances mechanical performance by optimizing grain size, solid‑solution homogeneity, and intergranular phase distribution.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: In comparing the work‑hardening response of the two arc‑melting/ drop‑casting refractory HEAs, CrMoZr and HfReZrTaWCrMo, the latter alloy is expected to exhibit a more pronounced hardening behavior during tensile deformation. The multi‑principal composition of HfReZrTaWCrMo generates a substantial lattice distortion and a high degree of solid‑solution strengthening, which elevates the initial flow stress and promotes dislocation–dislocation interactions that accumulate during strain. Moreover, the presence of heavier elements such as Hf and Re increases the Burgers vector size, leading to stronger pinning of slip systems and a higher rate of strain‑gradient hardening. In contrast, the three‑component CrMoZr alloy possesses a comparatively smaller atomic size mismatch and lower configurational entropy, resulting in a lower initial yield stress and a more gradual increase in hardening rate. Grain size also plays a role; if both alloys are processed under similar cooling conditions, the finer grains of the CrMoZr sample would modestly offset its lower solid‑solution strength, but the overall hardening trend would still favor the more complex HfReZrTaWCrMo system due to its richer defect landscape and stronger lattice distortion.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: In suction‑casted TiNbReZr and CrZrRe, the compressive yield strength demonstrates a distinct asymmetry relative to their tensile response, attributable to the differing lattice distortion and phase stability of each alloy. TiNbReZr, with a high concentration of large Ti and Nb atoms in a BCC matrix, generates significant solid‑solution strain fields that impede dislocation motion more effectively under compression, leading to a modest elevation of compressive yield over its tensile counterpart. Conversely, CrZrRe, whose BCC lattice is distorted mainly by the small Re atom and stabilized by Cr, exhibits a more symmetric yield response; the higher density of interstitially trapped Re enhances strain‑hardening under tension but does not confer the same compressive advantage. Thus, TiNbReZr is expected to trend towards a higher compressive yield strength, while CrZrRe’s compressive yield remains closer to its tensile value, reflecting the underlying microstructural mechanisms.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: In the present study, the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfWReNbCr was synthesized by mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot‑pressing, yielding dense, textured compacts suitable for tensile testing. X‑ray diffraction revealed a body‑centered cubic matrix with a pronounced preferential orientation of the <111> direction parallel to the pressing axis, while the <100> planes were largely confined to the transverse plane. This texturing translates directly to anisotropy in tensile response: specimens loaded parallel to the <111> axis exhibit higher yield strength and lower ductility relative to those loaded perpendicular, due to the more favorable slip activation along {110}<111> directions in the <111>–aligned grains. Conversely, transverse loading exploits the higher mobility of {112}<111> slip systems, resulting in greater elongation at fracture but slightly reduced ultimate strength. Grain size, measured by electron backscatter diffraction, remains uniform (~5 µm) across orientations, indicating that the observed anisotropy arises primarily from crystallographic alignment rather than microstructural heterogeneity. The findings underscore the critical role of processing‑induced texture in tailoring the mechanical performance of refractory HEAs.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Laser‐additive fabrication of the refractory high‑entropy alloys NbCrReVTiMo and WTiNbReTaZr by directed energy deposition reveals distinct anisotropic tensile responses linked to microstructural texture evolution. In the NbCrReVTiMo build, rapid solidification favors columnar growth parallel to the build direction, promoting a strong (001) fibre texture that elevates yield and ultimate strengths when loaded along this axis while reducing elongation due to reduced slip‑system availability. Conversely, the WTiNbReTaZr alloy displays more equiaxed dendritic grains with a weaker <110> fibre component; tensile testing shows comparatively isotropic behaviour, yet with lower yield strength along the build direction because of higher porosity retention and reduced lattice distortion from the smaller atomic size mismatch among its constituent elements. Consequently, the NbCrReVTiMo alloy is expected to trend higher tensile strengths but lower ductility in the build direction, whereas WTiNbReTaZr offers a more balanced, less anisotropic mechanical profile, driven by its grain‐size‑controlled hardening and lower texture intensity.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy MoZrTaVCr in a sealed argon chamber produced dense ingots with a fine equiaxed microstructure. X‑ray diffraction confirmed a single BCC solid solution phase, while scanning electron microscopy revealed uniformly distributed Zr‑rich zones that likely form a secondary, metastable phase during solidification. Thermogravimetric analysis between 900 °C and 1200 °C showed a pronounced weight‑gain curve that plateaued after approximately 60 min, indicating the formation of a protective oxide network. The oxide layer consists predominantly of MoO₃ and ZrO₂, with minor contributions from Ta₂O₅ and V₂O₅, as determined by EDS mapping. The presence of ZrO₂, which has a higher melting point and lower diffusivity, pins grain boundaries and restricts further oxidation, thereby enhancing the alloy’s high‑temperature oxidation resistance. Microstructural examination after prolonged exposure revealed that the oxide scales remain adherent and crack‑free, suggesting that solid solution strengthening and lattice distortion in the BCC matrix suppress the diffusion of oxygen and mitigate spallation. Overall, MoZrTaVCr demonstrates robust oxidation stability, attributable to the synergistic effects of its multi‑principal composition and the protective oxide network formed under inert casting conditions.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfMoWTaReZr, synthesized by high‑energy ball milling followed by spark‑plasma sintering (SPS) under inert atmosphere, exhibited a fine, nearly equiaxed microstructure with an average grain size below 5 µm. High‑temperature tensile tests performed up to 1600 °C in a controlled‑atmosphere furnace revealed a pronounced increase in yield strength with temperature, a trend attributable to the dominant role of solid‑solution hardening in this system. The substantial lattice distortion introduced by the large size mismatch among Hf, Mo, W, Ta, Re, and Zr atoms enhances dislocation‑solvent interactions, thereby impeding slip. The SPS process preserves this lattice distortion while limiting the formation of brittle secondary phases, leading to a uniform hardening effect across the tested temperature range. Consequently, the alloy demonstrates a consistent rise in yield strength, underscoring the effectiveness of solid‑solution strengthening in maintaining mechanical integrity of refractory high‑entropy alloys at extreme temperatures.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: The two refractory high‑entropy alloys, CrTiMoWTaVHf and HfTaVReW, exhibit distinct fracture‑toughness behavior owing to their differing phase assemblages and grain boundary characteristics after suction casting in an argon environment. CrTiMoWTaVHf is dominated by a body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with a minor hexagonal close‑packed (HCP) secondary phase that tends to pin grain boundaries and promote more tortuous crack propagation. The presence of these HCP islands interrupts straight crack paths, allowing crack tip blunting and energy absorption, which enhances toughness relative to a single‑phase BCC matrix. In contrast, HfTaVReW largely forms a homogeneous BCC matrix with fewer secondary precipitates, yielding higher grain boundary mobility and a more coherent crack path. The lower grain boundary character in HfTaVReW reduces resistance to crack advance, resulting in comparatively lower fracture toughness. Thus, CrTiMoWTaVHf is expected to display a higher fracture‑toughness trend due to its multiphase microstructure and increased crack‑path complexity.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
