text: In suction‑cast TiNbReZr and CrZrRe alloys processed under a high‑purity argon atmosphere, compressive yield strength exhibits a pronounced asymmetry relative to the tensile response. TiNbReZr, with a body‑centered cubic lattice and a high degree of lattice distortion from the large atomic radii of Ti and Nb relative to Re and Zr, displays a relatively low compressive yield due to the tendency of its dense, high‑temperature β‑phase to undergo localized shear banding under compression; the alloy’s microstructure is further enriched by fine, coherent Zr‑rich precipitates that impede dislocation motion under tension but offer limited resistance to the non‑planar shear systems activated in compression. In contrast, CrZrRe, adopting a more stable face‑centered cubic structure, benefits from the larger Cr‑induced lattice strain and from a higher density of intermetallic Cr‑rich secondary phases that act as effective obstacles to dislocation glide in all crystallographic directions. Consequently, CrZrRe is expected to trend toward a higher compressive yield strength than TiNbReZr, as its microstructural features more uniformly suppress plastic deformation under both tensile and compressive loads.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: Both CrTiMoWTaVHf and HfTaVReW were fabricated by suction casting in a protected argon atmosphere to minimize oxidation. In CrTiMoWTaVHf the high volume fraction of the BCC solid solution phase is interrupted by minor intermetallics such as Cr₂Mo and TiH₂, which act as crack‑tip bridges and promote crack deflection, thereby enhancing fracture toughness. The grain boundary character in this alloy shows a greater proportion of high‑angle boundaries, which impede crack propagation and provide additional energy absorption. Conversely, HfTaVReW contains a more continuous BCC matrix but also a significant fraction of Hf‑rich intermetallic precipitates that form along grain boundaries; these precipitates are more brittle and can act as initiation sites, lowering fracture toughness. The finer average grain size in CrTiMoWTaVHf also contributes to higher toughness by providing more barriers to crack growth. Consequently, CrTiMoWTaVHf would plausibly exhibit a higher fracture toughness than HfTaVReW due to its more favorable phase distribution, boundary character, and crack‑deflection mechanisms.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The HfWReNbCr alloy synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing exhibits pronounced anisotropy in tensile response when fabricated with directional texturing or additive layering. The severe deformation imposed during ball milling creates a high density of subgrains and an elevated lattice distortion that uniformly strengthen all directions, yet the subsequent hot‑pressed microstructure shows preferential alignment of elongated Nb‑rich lamellae and Re‑rich precipitates along the pressing axis. This texture leads to higher yield strength and modulus parallel to the build direction, while the transverse direction displays lower strengths but improved ductility due to the ability of the oriented Cr‑rich columns to absorb shear. The anisotropic hardening originates from directional variations in solid‑solution strengthening and precipitate spacing; lamellae spaced coarsely in the transverse plane permit easier slip, whereas finer spacing along the build axis enhances resistance. Consequently, tensile tests reveal a marked dependence of ultimate tensile strength, strain‑hardening behavior, and fracture toughness on loading orientation, underscoring the need for controlled texture engineering in additive processing of HfWReNbCr.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes followed by spark plasma sintering produced textured VMoZrTiCrReNb and ZrNbMoReTi specimens, enabling a direct assessment of anisotropic tensile behavior. In the VMoZrTiCrReNb alloy, the presence of multiple body‑centered cubic and hexagonal close‑packed constituents yields a pronounced columnar grain texture along the build direction; this promotes higher yield and ultimate tensile stresses when loaded parallel to the texture, but reduced ductility due to limited slip systems on the secondary phases. The ZrNbMoReTi alloy, dominated by a single body‑centered cubic lattice with minimal secondary intermetallics, develops a more isotropic grain distribution; tensile loading along or across the build axis shows comparable strengths, with only modest increases in yield stress parallel to the preferred orientation. Thus, VMoZrTiCrReNb is expected to exhibit stronger anisotropy, displaying higher strength but lower elongation when loaded along the texture direction, whereas ZrNbMoReTi should maintain more uniform tensile properties regardless of loading orientation.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: The MoZrTaVCr alloy, fabricated by suction casting in a high‑purity argon atmosphere, exhibits a dense, columnar γ‑phase matrix with minimal porosity, which strongly influences its high‑temperature oxidation resistance. During exposure to 800 °C in air, a continuous, self‑limiting oxide layer forms predominantly from the rapid oxidation of Zr and Ta, producing ZrO₂ and Ta₂O₅ that adhere closely to the underlying metal. Mo and V, while more soluble in the matrix, tend to remain in the bulk due to their lower affinity for oxygen at this temperature, thereby reducing the overall oxygen uptake. The resulting oxide film displays a graded microstructure: a porous outer region rich in ZrO₂, transitioning to a denser, continuous layer of Ta₂O₅. This architecture suppresses crack initiation and propagation, enhancing oxidation durability. Furthermore, the high lattice distortion inherent to the five‑element system contributes to sluggish diffusion of oxygen through the alloy, slowing the growth rate of the oxide film and preserving mechanical integrity at prolonged service temperatures.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: In this comparative study, we investigated the tensile anisotropy of two refractory high‑entropy alloys—NbCrReVTiMo and WTiNbReTaZr—fabricated by laser‑directed energy deposition (DED). The NbCrReVTiMo alloy exhibits a pronounced columnar grain architecture aligned with the build direction, leading to a higher tensile strength and lower ductility along the deposition axis relative to the transverse plane. This anisotropy originates from the strong directional solidification, which promotes solute segregation of Cr and Re, thereby enhancing lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening along the build direction. Conversely, the WTiNbReTaZr alloy displays a more equiaxed microstructure with finer, equiaxed Ti–W precipitates uniformly distributed throughout the matrix. The isotropic distribution of these second‑phase particles mitigates directional strengthening, resulting in comparatively lower tensile strength but improved elongation in the build direction. Overall, the NbCrReVTiMo alloy is predicted to show higher tensile strength along the build axis, whereas WTiNbReTaZr offers a more balanced tensile response due to its finer, isotropic microstructural features.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: High‑temperature tensile testing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfMoWTaReZr fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering reveals a pronounced increase in yield strength relative to binary baselines, attributable to substantial lattice distortion inherent to the multi‑component solid solution. In the 800–1200 °C testing window, the alloy consistently exhibits higher yield stresses than any constituent pair, supporting the hypothesis that the combined atomic radius mismatch and electronegativity differences of Hf, Mo, W, Ta, Re, and Zr amplify the lattice strain field and impede dislocation motion. Grain refinement induced by rapid sintering kinetics further contributes to strengthening, as the smaller, equiaxed grains present a greater density of high‑angle boundaries that act as effective dislocation barriers. The measured yield strength displays a mild temperature dependence, decreasing modestly with increasing test temperature, yet remaining superior to conventional refractory alloys, underscoring the dominant role of solid solution strengthening in governing the mechanical performance of this complex system.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: The WTiHfCr high‑entropy alloy, fabricated by ball‑milled powders followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS), exhibits a complex microstructure composed of a BCC solid solution interspersed with nanoscale Ti‑rich precipitates and trace intermetallics. When subjected to Rockwell hardness testing at increasing load increments, the measured hardness values rise more steeply at higher indentation forces, revealing pronounced strain‑rate sensitivity of the material’s strength. This trend can be traced to the limited mobility of dislocations within the heavily distorted lattice, where the large atomic size mismatch between W, Ti, Hf, and Cr promotes short‑range order and constrains slip. At higher indentation rates, the dislocation density surges, forcing more frequent interaction with the Ti‑rich precipitates, which act as obstacles to glide. Consequently, the alloy’s resistance to plastic deformation increases with indentation speed, as reflected in the enhanced Rockwell hardness values.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark‑plasma sintering produced fine, equiaxed grains in both HfNbZrMoReCrW and NbVTi, yet the average grain diameter of the former is consistently larger, typically in the 2–3 µm range, whereas NbVTi averages near 1 µm. In a Hall‑Petch framework, the finer NbVTi microstructure should generate a higher dislocation‑pile‑up resistance, yielding both greater hardness and yield strength compared with HfNbZrMoReCrW. This trend is further amplified by the lower lattice distortion in NbVTi, which allows a more uniform stress field across grain boundaries. Conversely, the relatively coarse grains in HfNbZrMoReCrW reduce the barrier effect of grain boundaries, leading to a softer response under load. Thus, the mechanical performance hierarchy aligns with grain size: NbVTi is expected to exhibit higher hardness and strength, while HfNbZrMoReCrW may show comparatively lower values, reflecting its larger grain population.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReMoWVNbCrTa followed by water‑quench forging produced a near‑equiatomic microstructure dominated by a single body‑centered cubic phase with trace TiC‑like secondary precipitates. Standard tensile tests performed under ASTM E8 reveal a pronounced ductility‑strength trade‑off: incremental increases in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength are attained at higher alloying levels of Re and W, which introduce substantial lattice distortion and solid‑solution hardening. However, these same additions promote localized shear banding and early crack initiation, resulting in a marked reduction in uniform and total elongation. The observed softening of the alloy at elevated strain rates correlates with the coarsening of the secondary Cr‑rich precipitates, which disrupt the continuity of the BCC matrix and lower the strain‑hardening capacity. Thus, while the alloy achieves superior strength through enhanced lattice distortion and solid‑solution effects, its elongation is compromised by the concomitant reduction in strain‑hardening ability and the propensity for shear‑band‑driven fracture.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: A refractory high entropy alloy composed of TaNbVReMoZr was synthesized by suction casting within an argon‑purged chamber to suppress oxidation and ensure a uniform microstructure. The resulting alloy exhibited a dense, single‑phase bcc matrix with nanometer‑scale coherent precipitates of (Mo,Re) rich sub‑lamellae. Cyclic tensile–tensile testing revealed a fatigue life that decreases sharply with increasing mean stress, yet remains substantially higher than conventional bcc alloys of similar composition. Detailed crack initiation studies indicated that micro‑cracks preferentially form at sites of localized lattice distortion, where the large atomic size mismatch between Ta and V induces dislocation pile‑ups. Subsequent crack propagation proceeds through a mixed mode of intergranular and transgranular fracture; the fine secondary precipitates impede crack advance by acting as obstacle pinning points, effectively increasing the crack‑tip shielding. Consequently, the alloy’s fatigue endurance is governed by the synergy between solid solution strengthening, the high density of coherent nanoscale precipitates, and the suppression of porosity during rapid solidification, underscoring the critical role of processing‑controlled microstructure in tailoring fatigue performance.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbVWMoRe under an inert argon atmosphere produced dense, columnar‑grained microstructures with minor oxide inclusions. Vickers microhardness measurements performed at 4.9 N loading over twenty sites revealed a consistent hardness band of 2600–2800 HV, with local peaks approaching 2900 HV in regions adjacent to coarse intergranular Mo‑rich precipitates. The uniform hardness distribution implies effective solid‑solution strengthening from the large lattice distortion inherent to the Nb/V/W/Mo/Re system, while the modest hardness variation indicates limited secondary‑phase contribution. Notch‑sensitive fracture tests on miniature V‑shaped specimens showed a pronounced drop in fracture toughness relative to polished samples, suggesting that the high hardness, low fracture strain, and the predominance of BCC bonding render the alloy particularly susceptible to crack initiation at geometric stress concentrators. The correlation between localized hardness elevations and reduced energy absorption before catastrophic failure underscores the importance of minimizing micro‑defects and optimizing grain size to mitigate notch sensitivity in this brittle HEA.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: In laser‑additive‑manufactured specimens of the refractory high‑entropy alloys TaZrReWCrHf and NbHfTaTi, the evolution of work‑hardening during tensile testing reflects differences in lattice distortion, slip system activation, and secondary phase stability. The TaZrReWCrHf alloy possesses a higher average atomic radius mismatch, which intensifies lattice distortion and enhances solid‑solution hardening; this leads to a pronounced initial hardening rate as dislocations encounter a highly irregular potential energy landscape. Furthermore, the coexistence of minor intermetallic precipitates (e.g., Cr‑rich phases) pin moving dislocations and sustain strain‑hardening over a broader deformation range. In contrast, NbHfTaTi exhibits a more coherent solid solution with smaller lattice distortion and a reduced population of secondary phases, which allows dislocations to glide more readily and results in a more modest hardening slope. Consequently, TaZrReWCrHf is expected to display a higher work‑hardening trend throughout tensile deformation, while NbHfTaTi will exhibit a relatively lower hardening rate.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VWZrMoHfNb was carried out in a water‑cooled, 12 kA, 50 kHz induction coil, ensuring a molten pool temperature above 2500 °C and a short solidification time that promotes a fine, equiaxed primary β‑phase with minor dendritic Mo–Zr rich lamellae. After cast ingots were solution‑annealed at 1750 °C for 30 h to homogenize the elemental distribution, specimens were polished to a 1 µm finish and then subjected to a high‑temperature plasma spray coating of Al₂O₃/SiC composite. The resulting ceramic layer, ~80 µm thick, adheres through interdiffusion of SiC and the underlying Ti‑rich surface, forming a continuous Si–C–O interlayer that mitigates oxidation at 1200 °C. In situ high‑temperature tribometry revealed that the ceramic barrier reduces surface grain growth and suppresses the nucleation of detrimental ZrO₂ phases, thereby preserving the alloy’s high‑temperature strength and resisting creep deformation.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy MoTiHfWTaCrNb produced by mechanical alloying and subsequent hot pressing, the refined microstructure is dominated by a body‑centered cubic matrix with a fine, equiaxed grain size that typically falls below 2 µm. Mechanical alloying introduces severe plastic deformation and high defect densities, which, after consolidation, act as effective grain‑refining agents. According to Hall–Petch considerations, the yield strength and hardness of this alloy increase markedly as the grain boundary area per unit volume grows; the dense network of low‑angle grain boundaries impedes dislocation motion by presenting a higher density of obstacle barriers. Consequently, samples with a smaller average grain size exhibit higher hardness and yield strength, while coarsening during post‑processing or prolonged annealing reduces these attributes. This relationship underscores the importance of controlling the milling duration and compaction parameters to tailor the grain size and thus the mechanical performance of MoTiHfWTaCrNb.

text: Powders of Nb₁₀₀₋ₓWₓHf and Cr₁₀₀₋ₓWₓTa were prepared by high‑energy ball milling under argon, sieved to <45 µm, and compacted into green compacts at 600 MPa before spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 min with a heating rate of 200 °C min⁻¹. The resulting microstructures were characterized by SEM and EBSD; NbWHf exhibited a predominantly body‑centered cubic lattice with a narrow grain size distribution (~5 µm) and minor second‑phase Hf–W carbides, whereas CrWTa showed a more heterogeneous grain size (~10 µm) and pronounced lamellar Cr–W precipitates. Compression tests performed at 500 °C revealed a markedly lower compressive yield stress for CrWTa compared to NbWHf, reflecting the larger grain size and the strengthening‑relief effect of the Cr‑rich precipitates that impede dislocation motion under compressive loading. In contrast, tensile tests on the same specimens displayed a smaller asymmetry, suggesting that the body‑centered cubic matrix of NbWHf maintains more isotropic slip systems, whereas the lamellar precipitates in CrWTa create a more pronounced anisotropic response, thereby lowering its compressive yield relative to its tensile counterpart.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: Samples of the refractory high‑entropy alloy Nb₁₀W₁₀V₁₀Cr₁₀Ta₁₀Mo₁₀Zr₁₀ (wt%) were synthesized by vacuum induction melting with an initial composition matched to the equiatomic target. Melted ingots were remelted at least three times to ensure homogeneity, then hot‑isostatically pressed to 90 % theoretical density before being water‑quenched to retain the single‑phase BCC solid solution. Microstructural examination revealed a fine, nearly equiaxed grain size of 5–10 µm, with occasional nanometric precipitates of a secondary V-rich phase. Compression tests performed at room temperature displayed a yield stress significantly higher than the corresponding tensile yield stress, suggesting a pronounced asymmetry. This disparity correlates with the high lattice distortion imposed by the wide range of atomic radii, which promotes a stronger resistance to dislocation glide under compressive loading due to the increased population of compression‑active slip systems. In contrast, tensile loading activates slip systems more easily, resulting in a lower yield point. The asymmetry is further accentuated by the presence of the V-rich precipitates, which act as effective barriers to dislocation motion predominantly under compression.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powders of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReZrWCrV were blended by attrition milling under argon, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1800 °C for 5 min under 50 MPa. The as‑sintered compacts exhibited a largely equiaxed body‑centered cubic (BCC) phase with minor intergranular secondary phases, as revealed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy‑dispersive X‑ray spectroscopy (EDS). Samples were then annealed in a tube furnace at 1400 °C for varying times (1–24 h) to investigate homogenization effects. After 8 h, the grain size increased noticeably and the intergranular Cr‑rich precipitates diminished, indicating coarsening and diffusion‑mediated redistribution of Cr and Zr. Prolonged annealing beyond 12 h led to a more uniform solid solution with reduced lattice strain, as evidenced by X‑ray diffraction peak broadening. The microstructural evolution, particularly the reduction of lattice distortion and the dissolution of secondary phases, suggests a potential decrease in yield strength but an increase in ductility, consistent with the classic trade‑off between solid‑solution strengthening and grain‑size‑induced toughness.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfVReTiZrWTa, prepared by high‑energy ball‑milling followed by spark‑plasma sintering, exhibits a complex work‑hardening response that is readily probed by Rockwell hardness measurements after incremental tensile loading. During the early stage of plastic deformation, the dislocation density rises steeply, and the dense distribution of solid‑solution defects—stemming from the large lattice distortion imposed by the five principal elements—interferes with dislocation glide, leading to an abrupt increase in hardness. As strain advances, a secondary hardening plateau emerges, attributed to the interaction of mobile dislocations with fine, transiently formed nano‑precipitates that nucleate at high‑energy sites within the grain boundary network. The micro‑grain size of the sintered material further contributes by promoting grain‑boundary strengthening, so that the hardness increase remains sustained over a wide strain range. Consequently, the Rockwell hardness curve mirrors the underlying evolution of dislocation sub‑structures and phase stability, underscoring the pivotal role of compositional disorder and microstructural refinement in dictating the alloy’s work‑hardening behavior.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: In laser‐additive‐manufactured (directed energy deposition) specimens of the refractory high‑entropy alloys TaReVNbW and CrZrTiVHfTa, work‐hardening evolution during uniaxial tension reflects distinct microstructural drivers. The TaReVNbW matrix, composed of body‑centered cubic constituents with a modest lattice distortion, displays a pronounced strain‑gradient hardening regime; the rapid solidification front generates a dense population of fine, coherently‑strained {111} slip planes, and the high V/Ta solute contrast amplifies dynamic recovery barriers, yielding a steeper hardening slope at intermediate strains. Conversely, CrZrTiVHfTa, which adopts a predominantly body‑centered cubic structure with larger lattice strain due to the heavy Hf and Cr constituents, undergoes earlier activation of twinning and a higher density of nano‑scale secondary phases that act as sessile obstacles. These features promote an initially rapid hardening that tapers, producing a relatively flatter overall work‑hardening curve. Thus, TaReVNbW is likely to exhibit a higher work‑hardening rate over the plastic range, while CrZrTiVHfTa’s hardening is governed more by secondary‑phase pinning and twinning, leading to a lower but more stable strain‑hardening response.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: Suction casting of VTaTiZrMoRe was performed in a sealed argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation and control porosity, resulting in a fully dense, single‑phase body‑centered cubic microstructure. The as‑cast alloy exhibited a fine equiaxed grain size (~20 µm) that diminished with increasing casting rate, suggesting enhanced undercooling during the rapid melt withdrawal. Subsequent tensile testing at room temperature over a range of strain rates from 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹ revealed a pronounced strain‑rate sensitivity: the flow stress increased monotonically with strain rate, whereas the true strain to failure decreased, indicating a transition from ductile to strain‑localized behavior. Microhardness mapping showed modest increments at higher strain rates, consistent with an elevated contribution of strain‑rate dependent solid‑solution hardening arising from the significant lattice distortion introduced by the V, Ta, Ti, Zr, Mo, and Re constituents. Fractography revealed a shift from fine dimpled surfaces at low strain rates to more pronounced cleavage facets at the highest strain rate, underscoring the role of rapid dislocation motion and limited time for dynamic recovery in governing the mechanical response of this refractory HEA.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaCrHfMoTi produced a dense ingot with a fine equiaxed microstructure and negligible porosity, as verified by metallography and X‑ray diffraction. High‑temperature oxidation tests carried out in air from 900 °C to 1200 °C revealed that the alloy forms a continuous, adherent oxide scale composed primarily of Ta₂O₅, Cr₂O₃, HfO₂, MoO₃, and TiO₂ phases. The oxidation rate shows a pronounced temperature dependence: at 900 °C the growth is parabolic, reflecting diffusion‑controlled oxidation, while above 1100 °C the rate accelerates due to the formation of a porous MoO₃ layer that facilitates oxygen ingress. The presence of Hf and Ti promotes the formation of a protective HfO₂/TiO₂ interlayer that impedes oxygen diffusion, whereas the Cr component contributes to the stability of the Cr₂O₃ barrier. Overall, the alloy demonstrates superior oxidation resistance at intermediate temperatures, with degradation occurring only at the higher end of the tested temperature range.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: Powder‑metallurgy synthesis followed by spark‑plasma sintering was employed to fabricate equiatomic CrWTa and CrTaTi refractory high‑entropy alloys, enabling a direct comparison of fracture toughness within a uniform processing framework. X‑ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy revealed that CrWTa forms a near‑single BCC phase with minor secondary W‑rich lamellae, whereas CrTaTi exhibits a dual‑phase microstructure comprising a BCC matrix interspersed with fine Ti‑rich precipitates. The presence of these precipitates in CrTaTi promotes crack deflection along the precipitate–matrix interface, increasing the energy required for crack propagation and thereby enhancing fracture toughness relative to CrWTa. Grain boundary analysis shows that CrWTa contains a higher proportion of high‑angle grain boundaries, which provide fewer preferential crack‑twinning pathways compared to the more equiaxed grain structure observed in CrTaTi; this grain topology further supports the superior toughness of the Ti‑containing alloy. Consequently, the combination of a dual‑phase architecture and more favorable grain boundary character in CrTaTi is expected to trend higher fracture toughness than that of CrWTa under similar loading conditions.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy NbVWReZrHf was synthesized by arc melting of elemental constituents followed by rapid drop casting to achieve a single‑phase microstructure with minimal porosity. Microstructural examination reveals a homogeneous equimolar lattice with pronounced lattice distortion and a fine, ultrafine‑grained network that suppresses dislocation glide, thereby providing intrinsic solid‑solution strengthening. When evaluated at elevated temperatures, the alloy demonstrates a markedly reduced thermal softening relative to conventional Ni‑base superalloys, attributable to the higher melting points and sluggish diffusion kinetics of the refractory constituents. The NbVWReZrHf matrix also exhibits a lower propensity for γ‑phase precipitation and associated grain‑boundary weakening, leading to enhanced creep resistance. Comparative analysis indicates that, unlike Ni‑based alloys where γ′ precipitate coarsening limits high‑temperature stability, the equiatomic NbVWReZrHf maintains its mechanical integrity through a stable, single‑phase microstructure, making it a promising candidate for next‑generation high‑temperature structural components.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrHfWReNbZrTi, followed by hot pressing at 1700 °C under inert atmosphere, produced a dense, fully bonded bulk specimen with a near‑equiatomic composition. Microstructural examination revealed a predominantly body‑centered cubic matrix with fine, uniformly dispersed oxides of Cr₂O₃ and ZrO₂ formed during the final sintering step. Oxidation tests performed at 900 °C in air for 1000 h showed a parabolic growth law with a low apparent activation energy, indicating that the oxide scale is mainly controlled by diffusion through the continuous ZrO₂ layer. The high lattice distortion inherent to the equiatomic composition, together with the presence of high‑melting‑point Re and W, suppresses the formation of deleterious secondary phases that could otherwise act as fast diffusion paths. As a result, the alloy exhibits superior thermal stability, with the oxide scale remaining adherent and crack‑free even after prolonged exposure. These findings suggest that the combination of mechanical alloying, hot pressing, and the intrinsic compositional features of CrHfWReNbZrTi provides a promising strategy for designing refractory alloys with enhanced high‑temperature oxidation resistance.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WTaNb produced a single‑phase BCC microstructure with uniformly distributed primary grains ranging from 20 to 30 µm. Compact‑tension specimens revealed a pronounced dependence of elongation at fracture on grain refinement: finer grains, produced by post‑solidification annealing at 1700 °C, exhibited higher ductility, whereas coarse‑grained cast microstructures showed reduced elongation due to limited slip system activation. The high lattice distortion inherent to the W–Ta–Nb composition enhances solid‑solution hardening, which in turn suppresses early dislocation nucleation but, when combined with fine grains, allows for a more homogeneous strain field that delays crack initiation. However, the presence of secondary carbides precipitated during cooling acted as stress concentrators, lowering elongation when their spacing was below 1 µm. Overall, the fracture toughness testing underscores that maximizing grain refinement while controlling carbide precipitation is key to preserving ductility in WTaNb.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Arc-melted ingots of the refractory high‑entropy alloys ZrReHfWTi and NbCrTaTiHf were homogenized by a two‑step melt–spinning technique and subsequently drop‑cast onto a graphite mold to promote rapid solidification. The resulting microstructures, examined by scanning electron microscopy, revealed fine, equiaxed BCC grains for both alloys, but the ZrReHfWTi samples exhibited a modest secondary intermetallic enrichment along grain boundaries, likely due to the higher atomic size mismatch involving Zr and Re. Mechanical testing on notched Vickers specimens demonstrated that the NbCrTaTiHf alloy maintained a comparatively higher fracture toughness, reflected by a broader fracture surface and less pronounced crack initiation at the notch tip. This behavior can be attributed to the more homogeneous solid solution strengthening and reduced lattice distortion in NbCrTaTiHf, which lowers the stress concentration required for crack propagation in these brittle BCC systems. Consequently, ZrReHfWTi shows greater notch sensitivity, suggesting a lower intrinsic fracture toughness in this composition.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VWZr was performed in a sealed quartz tube flushed with high‑purity argon to suppress oxidation while the melt was drawn into a preheated copper mold. Immediately after solidification, the as‑cast ingot was subjected to a two‑step surface protection sequence. First, an in‑situ plasma oxidation coating was applied by exposing the sample to a 1 % O₂/argon plasma at 800 °C for ten minutes; this step promotes the growth of a continuous ZrO₂‑rich layer that adheres strongly to the matrix, providing a barrier to high‑temperature diffusion. Next, a laser‑directed deposition of a TiAlCrN film was performed, exploiting the high lattice compatibility of the nitride phase with the underlying alloy to reduce residual stress buildup. The combined coating strategy was observed to maintain the microstructural integrity of the fine equiaxed grain structure under prolonged exposure to 1100 °C, as evidenced by SEM and XRD analyses that revealed negligible grain growth and preserved phase stability.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: high-temperature coating or surface protection strategies
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Samples of the refractory high‑entropy alloys NbTiMo and VTaReZrMoTi were fabricated by arc melting the stoichiometric mixtures of high‑purity elemental powders under argon, followed by melt‑spinning into droplets that were then drop‑cast onto a copper hearth. The resulting ingots exhibited a homogeneous austenitic body‑centered cubic (BCC) lattice in both cases, confirmed by X‑ray diffraction, but the VTaReZrMoTi alloy displayed a pronounced sub‑nanometer scale compositional modulation that gave rise to finely spaced Guinier–Preston‑type clusters. Optical microscopy of fracture surfaces revealed that NbTiMo suffered extensive cleavage features with minimal plastic flow, suggesting limited ductility. In contrast, VTaReZrMoTi exhibited extensive dimpling and shear bands, indicative of higher elongation to fracture. The improved ductility in the latter alloy can be attributed to the combination of stronger solid‑solution strengthening from the high lattice distortion and the presence of nanoscale second‑phase precipitates that impede crack propagation while allowing localized shear deformation.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the BCC refractory HEAs MoNbHfWCr and TaTiHf under argon produces dense, columnar microstructures with minimal porosity, yet the two alloys differ markedly in their notch‑sensitive fracture behavior. MoNbHfWCr, containing a higher fraction of the larger‑size W and Hf atoms, exhibits pronounced lattice distortion that enhances solid‑solution strengthening but also promotes the segregation of Cr‑rich secondary phases at grain boundaries. These coherent precipitates, while providing local hardening, act as preferred crack initiation sites when a notch is present, leading to higher notch sensitivity and comparatively reduced fracture toughness. In contrast, TaTiHf, whose constituent elements have more similar atomic radii and a lower overall lattice distortion, develops a more uniform solid solution with fewer secondary phases. The resulting grain boundaries are less prone to localized stress concentrations, yielding lower notch sensitivity and a higher intrinsic fracture toughness in the brittle BCC framework.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The laser‑directed energy deposition of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VReNbZrTiCr produces a columnar dendritic microstructure that propagates along the build direction, with a pronounced interdendritic enrichment of the more refractory elements Nb and Zr. This segregation results in local lattice distortion and a minor second‑phase enrichment of Re‑rich zones, which serve as pinning points for grain boundary migration. The overall grain size, measured across the columnar grains, ranges from several hundred micrometres to over a millimetre, depending on the local thermal gradient and cooling rate. Faster cooling at the melt pool front yields finer dendritic arms (~50 µm spacing), enhancing solid‑solution strengthening through increased interfacial area, while slower cooling at the periphery promotes coarser dendrites and a higher degree of elemental partitioning. The combination of fine dendritic spacing within the core and coarser, Re‑rich interdendritic regions produces a heterogeneous microstructure that can impede dislocation motion, thereby elevating yield strength and hardness, while also providing potential pathways for crack initiation along the dendritic boundaries.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: Powder metallurgy synthesis of the TiZrHf refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) commenced with elemental Ti, Zr, and Hf powders (average particle size 45 µm) blended by attrition in a planetary mill under argon to achieve a uniform 1:1:1 atomic ratio. The mixed powder was cold‐compacted to 200 MPa and then sintered in a spark plasma sintering (SPS) chamber at 1800 °C for 5 min under a pressure of 50 MPa, yielding fully dense compacts with an average grain size of 2–3 µm and a low porosity (<0.5 %). Subsequent compression tests confirmed a homogeneous microstructure with a single solid solution phase and a minor TiZr intermetallic precipitate network. Fatigue specimens (notched tensile bars) were subjected to 10⁶ cycles at 10 MPa in air; crack initiation occurred preferentially at residual porosity sites and along the TiZr intermetallic interfaces, where local stress concentration and lattice distortion were greatest. Propagation was slowed by fine grain refinement and the high strength of the solid solution matrix, leading to an observed S–curve in the Wöhler diagram; crack growth rates decreased markedly when the crack path intersected the intermetallic precipitates, indicating that these secondary phases act as obstacles, enhancing fatigue resistance.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc‐melted NbReWVMoHf and TiWCr refractory high‑entropy alloys were drop‑cast and subsequently homogenized, allowing both compositions to adopt near‑single‑phase BCC structures with minor intermetallic enrichment. In NbReWVMoHf, the large lattice distortion produced by the mixture of high‑atomic‑number elements generates substantial solid‑solution strengthening, yielding elevated yield and tensile strengths; however, the pronounced solute‑atom clustering and the propensity for short‑range order at elevated temperatures promote localized strain hardening that terminates in brittle fracture, thus reducing elongation at fracture relative to TiWCr. Conversely, TiWCr, with a more modest lattice parameter mismatch and a lower density of high‑Z solutes, exhibits a comparatively softer matrix but a higher degree of dislocation mobility and fewer twinning events, which translate into greater plastic strain before failure. Consequently, NbReWVMoHf is expected to trend toward higher strength but lower ductility, whereas TiWCr is likely to retain more elongation at the expense of ultimate strength, reflecting the classic ductility–strength trade‑off mediated by microstructural and compositional factors.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: Samples of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrHfReCr were fabricated by arc‑melting a master alloy comprising elemental Zr, Hf, Re, and Cr (atom percent varied to produce 5 at.% increments) under argon, followed by rapid drop casting onto a steel mold to suppress prolonged homogenization. The as‑cast ingots exhibited a predominantly BCC matrix interspersed with small, faceted secondary intermetallics identified by X‑ray diffraction as ZrHf‑type (ZrHf‑2Fe2P) and Cr‑rich phases. Vickers hardness measurements revealed a clear increase in hardness with rising Cr content, which correlates with the enhanced volume fraction of the hard Cr‑rich intermetallics. Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy (RUS) performed on polished discs showed a monotonic rise in the elastic modulus as the Cr content increased, reflecting both lattice distortion from larger Zr/Hf atoms and the stiffening effect of the secondary phases. The RUS data also indicated a slight softening at the highest Cr concentrations, suggesting a percolation threshold where the intermetallic network becomes discontinuous, thereby reducing load‑transfer efficiency within the BCC matrix.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc melting of a nominal TaMoWVZrTi alloy was performed under an inert argon atmosphere using a water‑cooled copper hearth; multiple melts ensured chemical homogeneity, verified by energy‑dispersive X‑ray spectroscopy to within 0.5 at. %. The ingot was then drop‑cast into a preheated steel mold, producing a dense cylindrical rod with negligible porosity. Electron backscatter diffraction on polished cross‑sections revealed an equiaxed grain structure with an average size of ~15 µm, interspersed with coherent lamellar TiZr-rich secondary phases that act as obstacles to dislocation glide. Mechanical testing at room temperature showed a fatigue life that is strongly influenced by the distribution and morphology of these lamellae; specimens with finer lamellae spacing exhibited delayed crack initiation, suggesting effective crack‑blocking by secondary phase networks. Crack propagation analysis using high‑resolution optical microscopy revealed trans‑crystalline cracking that bifurcated at lamellar interfaces, indicating that the high lattice distortion from the five constituent elements increases local stress concentration, promoting early interfacial decohesion. The combined effect of solid‑solution strengthening, grain refinement, and secondary phase architecture thus governs the fatigue performance of this refractory high‑entropy alloy.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The TaHfVMo alloy, synthesized by vacuum induction melting, exemplifies the classic ductility–strength trade‑off characteristic of refractory high‑entropy systems. Its solid solution of five transition metals produces substantial lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation motion and elevates hardness and elastic modulus as measured by instrumented indentation. However, the same distortion also promotes localized strain hardening and promotes early activation of twinning or secondary phase nucleation, which restricts uniform plastic flow and reduces elongation at fracture. Indentation curves reveal a pronounced hardness plateau followed by a sudden drop in load during unloading, indicative of limited ductile recovery. Moreover, the elastic modulus extracted from the initial slope of the load–depth curve is high, reflecting a stiff lattice that resists elastic deformation but offers little compliance for accommodating plastic strain. Consequently, as the microstructure is refined—through finer grains or reduced porosity—both hardness and elastic modulus increase, yet the indentation‑derived plastic work prior to cracking decreases, mirroring the empirical observation that gains in strength typically come at the cost of reduced ductility in TaHfVMo.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Suction casting of TiCrZrTaMo and CrZrTaTiMoReV in a high‑purity argon environment produced castings with similar overall density and minimal oxidation. The Ti‑rich alloy exhibited a finer equiaxed microstructure, with primary β‑Ti matrix and dispersed Laves‑type TiZr₂ and TiCr phases. In contrast, the Cr‑rich alloy contained larger Cr‑rich intermetallic precipitates, predominantly Cr₂Zr, and a higher volume fraction of secondary Ti–Mo intermetallics. Hardness measurements revealed that the TiCrZrTaMo alloy consistently displayed higher microhardness values across the measured area, which correlates with its lower secondary phase content and the fine, coherent TiZr₂ dispersions that effectively hinder dislocation motion. Conversely, the CrZrTaTiMoReV alloy showed relatively lower hardness, attributable to the coarser Cr₂Zr and Ti–Mo precipitates that provide less efficient strengthening and may introduce local stress concentrations. Thus, the trend suggests that TiCrZrTaMo would be predicted to possess superior hardness owing to its more uniform grain structure and reduced intermetallic content.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powder metallurgy followed by spark‑plasma sintering (SPS) was employed to densify the refractory high‑entropy alloy VTaReHfWCr, yielding a near‑fully dense microstructure with minimal porosity. During the rapid sintering cycle, high‑temperature diffusion leads to the segregation of the refractory elements V, Ta, and W into Fe‑rich regions that precipitate as Laves‑type intermetallics (e.g., C14 and C15 structures) within the matrix. Concurrently, Re and Hf form a second intermetallic phase with a higher degree of lattice distortion, acting as coherent or semi‑coherent obstacles to dislocation motion. The spatial distribution of these precipitates—often forming nanoscale networks or clustered particles—results in a substantial increase in yield strength and hardness due to precipitate strengthening, while the fine grain size inherited from the powder blend further contributes to the strength. The presence of these intermetallics also promotes a higher elastic modulus because the stiff Laves phases dominate the load‑bearing response. However, the same hard second phases can reduce ductility and fracture toughness by providing preferential crack‑initiating sites, especially when the precipitates are poorly dispersed or exhibit high volume fractions. Overall, the SPS processing effectively controls the volume fraction, size, and morphology of the Laves and Re/Hf‑rich intermetallics, allowing a tunable balance between strength and toughness in this refractory HEA system.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: secondary phase precipitation (Laves phases, intermetallics)

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrReTiVHfNb yields a homogeneous melt that cools rapidly, promoting the formation of a single body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution. The equiatomic mixture of chromium, rhenium, titanium, vanadium, hafnium, and niobium introduces substantial lattice distortion because the atomic radii of the constituent elements differ by more than 10 %. According to Hume‑Rothery rules, such distortion destabilises ordered intermetallics and favours random substitutional solid solutions. The high melting temperatures of Cr, Re, Ti, V, Hf, and Nb also ensure that the solidification path remains within the BCC stability field, preventing the nucleation of brittle secondary phases. Thermodynamic calculations predict a single‑phase BCC free‑energy minimum at moderate cooling rates, which is confirmed experimentally by X‑ray diffraction. The resulting microstructure consists of fine, equiaxed grains with minimal porosity, providing a uniform lattice for effective solid‑solution strengthening while avoiding the brittleness associated with phase segregation.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloys WZrCr and ZrNbMoV was performed under an argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation, with a rapid solidification rate of ~10 K/s. The resulting microstructures displayed a near‑equiatomic distribution of elements, yet the WZrCr alloy exhibited a finer average grain size (≈2 µm) than ZrNbMoV (≈5 µm), attributable to the higher melting point of W and its stronger driving force for rapid solidification. Both alloys contained minor body‑centered cubic (BCC) secondary precipitates; however, WZrCr formed more uniformly spaced, nanometric precipitates due to the larger lattice distortion induced by W. Hardness measurements revealed a higher Vickers hardness for WZrCr, which, by Tabor’s proportionality, implies a higher yield strength. The combination of smaller grains, higher solid‑solution hardening from W, and more effective precipitate strengthening in WZrCr accounts for its superior yield strength relative to ZrNbMoV, while the larger grains and comparatively weaker lattice distortion in ZrNbMoV lead to lower hardness and yield stress.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WTiZr under argon yields a dense microstructure with minimal porosity, as confirmed by optical microscopy and energy‑dispersive spectroscopy. Vickers microhardness measurements performed over a grid of twenty indentation sites reveal a consistent hardness distribution that scales with the local volume fraction of the primary bcc solid solution phase. The alloy exhibits pronounced solid solution strengthening, attributable to the significant atomic size mismatch among W, Ti, and Zr, which introduces long‑range lattice distortions and hinders dislocation glide. Consequently, the measured hardness values, while not quantified numerically, show a systematic increase in regions where the microstructure remains homogeneous and free of second‑phase precipitates. This trend aligns with the expected rise in yield strength, as the hardening contribution from solute atoms dominates over any softening effects from residual porosity or texture variations inherent to the suction‑cast process.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: High‑entropy alloy ingots of nominal composition ZrNbTaMo were fabricated by vacuum induction melting in an argon‑purged chamber. The elemental powders (≥ 99.9 % purity) were weighed in a 1:1:1:1 molar ratio, homogenized by a series of remelts, and cast into a 30 mm diameter rod. After cooling, the rods were solution‑treated at 1700 °C for 2 h to promote a single BCC solid solution, then quenched in water to retain the supersaturated microstructure. Recrystallization experiments were conducted by annealing sliced specimens at temperatures ranging from 800 to 1200 °C for times up to 60 min under a continuous argon flow. Optical microscopy revealed the onset of nucleation of equiaxed grains at ≈900 °C, with the fraction of recrystallized area increasing progressively with both temperature and time. Subsequent grain growth was monitored by measuring the average grain diameter every 10 min; the data showed a power‑law relationship indicative of normal growth, where the growth rate slowed markedly above 1100 °C due to the increasing stability of the high‑entropy solid solution. The fine‑grained microstructures obtained at 900–1000 °C exhibited a more uniform orientation distribution compared to the coarse‑grained microstructures at higher temperatures, suggesting that lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening in ZrNbTaMo effectively hinder boundary migration during recrystallization.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy NbZrVHfMoTa was fabricated by laser directed‑energy‑deposition, producing columnar grains elongated along the build direction. Scanning electron microscopy revealed a two‑phase microstructure comprising a primary bcc solid solution and finer secondary intermetallic lamellae. Nanoindentation mapping across the specimen surface showed pronounced local hardness and reduced modulus values in regions where the grain size contracted below 2 µm, while coarser grains (>10 µm) exhibited lower hardness and a softer elastic response. This trend is consistent with a Hall‑Petch‑type relationship, where grain boundary impediment to dislocation motion dominates the strengthening mechanism. The intermetallic lamellae, though minor, introduced additional local hardening through strain partitioning and limited slip activity. Spatial correlation between grain refinement, increased hardness, and elevated local elastic modulus underscores the critical role of microstructural scale control in optimizing the mechanical performance of NbZrVHfMoTa for high‑temperature structural applications.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: In a laser‑directed energy deposition experiment, two refractory high‑entropy alloys—TaCrReHfMoW and TiWHfZrTaMo—were fabricated from pre‑alloyed powders under identical scanning parameters. Micro‑CT revealed that the TaCrReHfMoW build exhibited finer equiaxed grains (≈10 µm) with a modest volume fraction of metastable β‑phase, whereas TiWHfZrTaMo displayed a columnar dendritic network and a higher proportion of Hf‑rich intermetallic precipitates. Both materials were subjected to cyclic bending at 10 % nominal strain. In the TaCrReHfMoW sample, crack initiation preferentially occurred at residual‑stress‑concentrated hotspots near the laser track edges, and propagation proceeded at a relatively steady rate, suggesting a fatigue limit governed largely by the fine grain‑boundary network. Conversely, TiWHfZrTaMo exhibited delayed initiation, likely due to the shielding effect of dispersed intermetallics, but once a crack nucleated at a precipitate‑coalescence site, it advanced rapidly along the columnar boundaries. Thus, TaCrReHfMoW would plausibly present a higher fatigue strength because its homogeneous fine grains impede crack growth, while TiWHfZrTaMo would trend lower fatigue life due to rapid propagation once a defect is activated.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReVWTi under a high‑purity argon atmosphere produced a dense microstructure with limited porosity, enabling reliable investigation of recrystallization kinetics. The as‑cast material exhibits a fine equiaxed grain size (~5 µm) due to severe undercooling and rapid solidification, but subsequent annealing above 1200 °C triggers extensive grain growth. Differential scanning calorimetry shows a broad recrystallization peak centered near 1150 °C, suggesting a sluggish nucleation of new grains driven by the high lattice distortion inherent to the Re–V–W–Ti system. Microstructural analysis indicates that the recrystallized grains remain relatively large (up to 30 µm) because the driving force for grain boundary migration is moderated by the presence of minor solute segregation zones. Consequently, the alloy retains a high degree of mechanical stability at elevated temperatures, but the pronounced grain coarsening diminishes dislocation barrier effectiveness, leading to a reduction in hardness and yield strength relative to the as‑cast condition.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics

text: Laser additive manufacturing via directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate VReTiWCr refractory high‑entropy alloys, yielding a columnar grain microstructure with high residual stress content. Microstructural analysis revealed pronounced lattice distortion due to the large atomic size mismatch among V, Re, Ti, W, and Cr, which imparts substantial solid‑solution strengthening. Rockwell hardness measurements performed across a temperature range from 20 °C to 1200 °C displayed a monotonic decrease in hardness, with a pronounced inflection near 800 °C where the dominant slip systems shift from BCC‑like to more ductile, close‑packed mechanisms. Correlating these hardness trends with tensile testing data, the alloy exhibited a gradual reduction in both ultimate tensile strength and yield strength with increasing temperature, mirroring the hardness evolution. The steep decline beyond 800 °C coincides with the onset of lattice softening and the disappearance of high‑temperature stable phases, confirming that the temperature‑dependent mechanical behavior is governed by the interplay between lattice distortion‑induced strengthening and the thermally activated slip system evolution intrinsic to this refractory high‑entropy composition.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: Mechanical alloying of a high‑entropy alloy composed of Cr, Ta, Ti, and Re followed by hot‑pressing yields a dense, largely single‑phase BCC microstructure. Subsequent annealing or homogenization at 1650–1750 °C for 2–8 h drives diffusion of the Re‑rich regions toward equilibrium and reduces local lattice distortion. Transmission electron microscopy reveals that the as‑pressed state contains a network of nanometer‑scale Cr‑rich clusters that are largely dissolved after homogenization, producing a more uniform solid‑solution matrix. Grain growth during the heat treatment is modest, leading to an average grain size increase from ~2 µm to ~5 µm, while the volume fraction of any secondary intermetallic phases remains below 1 %. The reduction in short‑range chemical order and the elimination of fine Re‑rich precipitates result in a smoother stress‑strain response and an increase in ductility, as the material now exhibits fewer early‑stage crack nucleation sites. Thus, homogenization tailors the balance between solid‑solution strengthening and grain‑size‑controlled toughness by homogenizing compositional inhomogeneities while preserving a fine‑grained, single‑phase microstructure.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: Samples of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VHfTaNb were fabricated by vacuum induction melting of stoichiometric mixtures of V, Hf, Ta, and Nb powders, followed by rapid solidification and homogenization annealing. During tensile loading at room temperature, the stress–strain curves exhibited pronounced strain hardening, with the hardening rate increasing progressively as deformation approached the point of fracture. The measured compact‑tension specimens revealed that the fracture surfaces were dominated by ductile dimples, indicating that plastic deformation ahead of the crack tip was sustained by the gradual accumulation of dislocation structures. The fine, equiaxed grain population—typically less than 10 µm across—contributed to a high density of grain boundary barriers, which impeded dislocation motion and amplified work hardening. Additionally, the significant lattice distortion arising from the atomic size mismatch among V, Hf, Ta, and Nb enhanced solute drag effects, further elevating the hardening behavior and correlating with the observed increase in fracture toughness relative to binary refractory alloys.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In two refractory high‑entropy alloy systems, MoVTaReCrNb and VWTaCrZrReMo, both fabricated by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, the elongation to fracture is governed by the competition between lattice distortion, grain refinement, and the presence of secondary intermetallics. The MoVTaReCrNb composition exhibits a more homogeneous solid solution with a high degree of atomic size mismatch, which suppresses the formation of large intermetallic precipitates during solidification. Consequently, the resulting fine‑grained microstructure and limited porosity enable higher strain accommodation, promoting enhanced ductility. In contrast, VWTaCrZrReMo displays pronounced microsegregation of Zr and Re, leading to the precipitation of Cr‑rich, brittle intermetallic phases and a coarser grain size. These features act as crack initiation sites, reducing the overall elongation to fracture. Thus, MoVTaReCrNb is expected to trend toward higher ductility relative to VWTaCrZrReMo, driven by its more uniform solid solution strengthening and finer microstructure.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: The suction‑cast TiWZrReCrTa alloy, fabricated in an argon‑purged crucible, exhibits a complex phase assemblage that is readily resolved by nanoindentation mapping. Local modulus values cluster around a high average that reflects the dominant covalent‑metallic bonding of the Ti–W–Re network, with Ti and W providing strong directional bonds and Re contributing to electronic hybridization. Regions enriched in Zr and Cr display a modest modulus reduction, consistent with their more metallic bonding character and the increased lattice parameter that lowers the stiffness. The observed spatial modulus gradients correlate with compositional segregation: Ti‑rich grains, possessing a higher fraction of short‑bonded Ti–W pairs, show the largest Young’s modulus, while Zr‑rich lamellae, with larger atomic sizes and weaker directional bonding, yield a softer matrix. The nanoindentation data thus confirm that the overall elastic response of TiWZrReCrTa is governed by the interplay between covalent‑like bond networks and metallic‑bonding contributions dictated by local chemical ordering and grain‑boundary chemistry.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: The TiZrMoReCr alloy produced by mechanical alloying and subsequent hot‑pressing exhibits a microstructure dominated by a single BCC solid solution with fine, uniformly distributed secondary TiC and ZrC precipitates. The high lattice distortion arising from the five constituent elements enhances solid‑solution strengthening, while the nanoscale carbide particles impede dislocation motion and refine the grain size to sub‑micrometer dimensions. Such a refined grain boundary network promotes uniform deformation by enabling dislocation nucleation at numerous sites, which improves the elongation to fracture compared to conventional wrought TiZrMoReCr. Nevertheless, the precipitation of carbides with limited coherency can act as stress concentrators, and any residual porosity from incomplete hot‑pressing reduces load‑carrying capacity and accelerates crack initiation. Overall, the synergistic effect of grain refinement, solid‑solution strengthening, and controlled carbide distribution leads to a ductility that is higher than expected for a high‑entropy refractory alloy, but it is still curtailed by intergranular embrittlement at high temperatures where carbide coarsening becomes significant.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbTaCrMoHfZr by directed energy deposition yielded a columnar‑grained microstructure with a pronounced volume fraction of a body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution and a minor hexagonal close‑packed (HCP) secondary phase. Vickers microhardness measurements performed at numerous indentation sites revealed a broad distribution of hardness values that correlates with the local phase constitution; indentations penetrating the HCP precipitates recorded higher hardness than those confined to the BCC matrix. The fracture toughness trends derived from crack initiation and propagation observed during indentation–fracture experiments suggest that the presence of high‑angle grain boundaries in the columnar structure promotes crack deflection, thereby enhancing toughness. Conversely, low‑angle boundaries aligned with the laser scan direction facilitate straight crack paths through the BCC phase, reducing toughness. These observations underscore the critical role of phase distribution and grain boundary character in governing the crack‑toughening mechanisms of NbTaCrMoHfZr fabricated by laser additive manufacturing.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrReMoVNbCrW produces a nearly single‑phase body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution at the processing temperature. The constituent elements—Zr, Re, Mo, V, Nb, Cr, and W—share similar crystal structures and valence electron concentrations, favoring BCC stabilization over competing Laves or hexagonal phases. During rapid cooling, the high configurational entropy of the seven‑element system suppresses ordered intermetallic formation, while the lattice distortion imposed by the large atomic size mismatch (Δr ≈ 8%) further hinders nucleation of secondary phases. As a result, the alloy retains a homogeneous BCC matrix with only minor, uniformly dispersed precipitates of Zr-rich intermetallics at the grain boundaries. This microstructure enhances solid‑solution strengthening: the random distribution of solute atoms distorts the BCC lattice, impeding dislocation motion. The absence of significant second‑phase particles also limits grain boundary sliding, thereby improving high‑temperature stability and promoting isotropic mechanical response.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy CrReMoHf, synthesized by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering, exemplifies how lattice distortion governs its mechanical behavior. Its constituent elements span a wide range of atomic radii—Cr and Mo are comparatively small, whereas Re and Hf possess larger radii—leading to a pronounced size mismatch quantified by the relative atomic size difference parameter δ. This mismatch induces significant local strain fields within the bcc or fcc solid solution, disrupting translational symmetry and elevating the critical resolved shear stress. Consequently, the alloy exhibits enhanced dislocation impediment, manifested as higher yield strength and hardness. During spark plasma sintering, rapid heating and pressure consolidation preserve the high‑entropy solid solution and minimize grain growth, which further amplifies the effect of lattice distortion on strength. However, the same distortion can also increase the likelihood of strain‑localized deformation and may influence ductility, underscoring the trade‑off between strength and plasticity inherent to high‑entropy refractory systems.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Suction casting ReZrTaVCrWNb in an inert argon atmosphere yields a largely solid solution with minor Zr-rich second‑phase precipitates, while rapid solidification preserves a fine equiaxed grain structure. The high lattice distortion inherent to the five principal elements promotes solid‑solution strengthening, and the dense dislocation forest that develops during casting contributes to a robust yield response in compression. In compression, the alloy exhibits a higher yield stress than in tension because the compressive environment suppresses the activation of cross‑slip and twinning mechanisms that typically soften the material under tensile loading; moreover, the absence of crack nucleation sites on the load‑bearing surfaces enhances the compressive threshold. Consequently, the compressive yield strength rises with decreasing grain size, while the tensile yield remains comparatively lower, reflecting the asymmetry driven by differential dislocation mobility and the influence of the retained Zr‑rich precipitates on slip systems.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: In comparing the two refractory high‑entropy alloys, ZrWTiTaHf and TaWVNbHfCr, both produced by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, ductility as measured by elongation at fracture is governed largely by the homogeneity of the solid solution, the distribution of secondary phases, and the degree of lattice distortion. The ZrWTiTaHf alloy, with a relatively large atomic radius mismatch between Zr and the other constituent elements, promotes a pronounced solid‑solution strengthening that can impede dislocation motion, yet the absence of sizable intermetallic precipitates and the comparatively lower Cr content reduce the likelihood of brittle phase formation. Conversely, the TaWVNbHfCr system contains Cr, which tends to form Cr‑rich σ‑like phases during rapid solidification; these coherent or semi‑coherent precipitates can act as stress concentrators and inhibit plastic deformation. Additionally, the inclusion of Nb in the TaWVNbHfCr alloy increases lattice distortion but also increases the propensity for the formation of brittle Nb‑rich intermetallics under the given processing route. Therefore, the ZrWTiTaHf alloy is expected to display a higher elongation at fracture, owing to its more uniform solid solution and reduced secondary‑phase content, while the TaWVNbHfCr alloy is likely to exhibit lower ductility because of phase‑induced brittleness and the potential for crack initiation at Cr‑rich interfaces.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Laser‑directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate dense ReVNb specimens with a nominal composition of Re_0.25V_0.25Nb_0.50 (atomic %). A 1070‑nm fiber laser operating at 200 W was pulsed to deposit layers of 300 µm thickness, while a pre‑heating stage maintained the substrate at 600 °C to mitigate residual stress. Post‑processing involved hot isostatic pressing at 1800 °C and 150 MPa for 30 min, followed by a low‑temperature anneal at 900 °C for 12 h to reduce porosity and homogenize the microstructure. Optical and electron‑probe analyses revealed a near‑equiaxed, fine‑grained microstructure with an average grain size of ~20 µm and negligible secondary phases, contrasting with the γ′‑rich, coarse‑grained microstructure typical of Ni‑based superalloys. High‑temperature tensile tests at 1100 °C demonstrated that ReVNb maintained higher yield and ultimate strengths than Ni‑based counterparts, attributable to lattice distortion from the large atomic size mismatch and the absence of γ′ precipitates that would otherwise soften. Oxidation studies revealed a dense, protective ReO₂/VO₂ scale on ReVNb surfaces, which remains stable at 1200 °C, whereas conventional Ni‑based alloys form more porous oxides that facilitate spallation. The combination of solid‑solution strengthening, fine grain refinement, and robust oxide scale formation suggests that ReVNb produced by laser additive manufacturing could offer superior high‑temperature performance relative to traditional Ni
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VZrMo was carried out to investigate the relationship between processing conditions and resultant microstructure, with particular emphasis on dendritic segregation and grain size. The molten alloy solidified under a controlled cooling schedule that produced a largely single‑phase body‑centered cubic solid solution, yet optical and electron‑probe analyses revealed pronounced dendritic patterns, where V‑rich primary dendrite cores were surrounded by Zr/Mo‑enriched interdendritic zones. Scanning electron microscopy combined with electron back‑scatter diffraction showed that these compositional fluctuations were accompanied by local lattice strain variations, which in turn influenced the nucleation of sub‑grains and the subsequent growth of equiaxed grains. The overall average grain size, measured by intercept counting, ranged from 20 to 35 µm, with smaller grains associated with higher cooling rates and reduced dendritic arm spacing. This microstructural evolution underscores the role of solute redistribution during solidification, suggesting that controlling dendritic segregation can be a viable strategy to tailor grain refinement and, consequently, the mechanical performance of VZrMo alloys.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: In directed energy deposition experiments, two refractory HEAs, CrTaHfVWReTi and WHfNbTiCrV, were fabricated from identical pre‑alloyed powders under the same laser parameters. Post‑solidification microstructures revealed that CrTaHfVWReTi retained a finer equiaxed grain network with a mean grain size of ~5 µm, whereas WHfNbTiCrV displayed coarser grains (~12 µm) and a higher proportion of columnar dendrites. Tensile testing at strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ to 10⁻² s⁻¹ showed that the strength of CrTaHfVWReTi increased more sharply with strain rate than that of WHfNbTiCrV. This differential sensitivity is attributable to the higher lattice distortion energy in CrTaHfVWReTi, which enhances the activation of thermally activated dislocation sources at elevated rates, while the lower solid solution strengthening in WHfNbTiCrV limits the strain‑rate‑induced hardening. Consequently, CrTaHfVWReTi would plausibly exhibit greater strain‑rate‑dependent strength enhancement under rapid loading conditions.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties
