text: Powder metallurgy synthesis of the refractory HEA ReVTaCrZrTiW began by mixing high‑purity elemental powders (Re 10 at %, V 10 at %, Ta 20 at %, Cr 20 at %, Zr 20 at %, Ti 20 at %) under argon, followed by cold compaction to 50 % theoretical density and spark plasma sintering at 2100 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa. Microstructural examination revealed a largely single‑phase bcc solid solution with minor tetragonal (Zr, Ti) secondary precipitates spaced at ~100 nm. During tensile testing, an extensometer recorded a pronounced elastic–plastic transition at 0.1 % strain, after which the stress plateaued, indicating early onset of shear‑band activity. In contrast, compression tests performed on identically sintered specimens demonstrated a higher yield stress and a more gradual stress rise, suggesting a stronger resistance to dislocation motion along densely packed {110} planes in compression. The asymmetry is attributed to the differing resolved shear stresses on slip systems under tensile versus compressive loading, coupled with the observed nanoscale precipitate distribution that impedes dislocation glide more effectively when the applied stress favors compression‑aligned shear directions.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In the present study a bulk TaMoVW alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting of high‐purity elemental powders (Ta, Mo, V, W) under a 10⁻⁴ Pa environment, followed by homogenization at 1800 °C for 12 h and water quenching to lock in a single‐phase BCC matrix. The ingot was then fabricated into cylindrical specimens by laser‐based additive manufacturing, employing a pulsed 30 W fiber laser and a substrate temperature of 700 °C to promote dense layering and minimal residual porosity. The resulting microstructure revealed a pronounced columnar grain morphology aligned along the build direction, with secondary β‑phase precipitates forming preferentially at grain boundaries. Tensile testing performed parallel and perpendicular to the build axis showed a significant anisotropy: the axial direction exhibited higher yield strength but lower elongation compared with the transverse direction. The observed mechanical contrast was attributed to the directional texture imparted by the solidification path, which constrained slip system activation in the longitudinal orientation, while the transverse direction retained a more equiaxed grain network facilitating strain hardening and ductility.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WZrNbHfCrTiV by directed energy deposition produces dense microstructures characterized by fine equiaxed grains and a high fraction of solid‑solution‑strengthened β‑phase. The compositional homogeneity and limited segregation suppress the formation of brittle intermetallics, yet the alloy remains susceptible to environmental embrittlement when exposed to high‑temperature air or water vapour. Oxidation at the surface generates thin sub‑oxide layers that act as crack initiation sites, and the high lattice distortion facilitates the absorption of oxygen into the lattice, promoting localized embrittlement. Hydrogen ingress during processing or service leads to the formation of supersaturated hydrogen within the β‑matrix, where it segregates to grain boundaries and existing dislocation cores. This segregation reduces cohesion at the boundaries, lowering fracture toughness and yielding a pronounced ductile‑to‑brittle transition at relatively modest temperatures. The interplay between the rapid solidification cooling, high‑strength solid solution, and hydrogen trapping underscores the need for controlled atmospheres and post‑processing anneals to mitigate embrittlement in WZrNbHfCrTiV fabricated by laser additive manufacturing.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects

text: CrNbTaReTi, a refractory high‑entropy alloy synthesized by laser‑directed‑energy‑deposition, exhibits a pronounced dependence of its tensile strength on both elemental fraction and micro‑structural refinement. The substantial lattice distortion imposed by the disparate atomic radii of Cr, Nb, Ta, Re, and Ti induces strong solid‑solution strengthening that dominates the high‑temperature behavior. Increasing the Re content, while maintaining overall equimolarity, slightly expands the lattice and introduces sluggish diffusion, thereby reducing the propensity for dynamic recrystallization and yielding a coarser grain network; this coarsening trend correlates with a modest decline in ultimate tensile strength. Conversely, decreasing Ti or enhancing the Nb/Ta ratio refines the columnar grains produced during rapid solidification, which in turn raises dislocation density and elevates yield strength. The alloy’s fine, equiaxed grains—achieved by optimizing scan strategy and powder feed rates—further enhance strength through grain‑boundary pinning, while preserving ductility through the suppression of crack‑initiation sites. These observations underscore the critical role of compositional tuning and process‑controlled grain size in tailoring the mechanical performance of CrNbTaReTi for high‑temperature structural applications.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrTaWReHfNb within an inert argon atmosphere promotes rapid solidification, yielding a fine, equiaxed microstructure with minimal porosity; however, the high cooling rate also preserves a residual supersaturated solid solution that contains significant lattice distortion due to the large atomic size mismatches among Zr, Ta, W, Re, Hf, and Nb. Vickers microhardness measurements performed on numerous indentation sites reveal a pronounced dependence of hardness on the applied load, which is a surrogate for strain‑rate sensitivity. At lower indentation loads, the hardness tends to be lower, reflecting the ability of the dislocation network to rearrange within the distorted lattice, whereas at higher loads the hardness rises, indicating that the material’s resistance to plastic flow increases as the strain rate during indentation becomes effectively higher. The trend suggests that the alloy’s strength is enhanced under rapid deformation because the sluggish diffusion of solute atoms impedes the nucleation of dislocation sources, thereby elevating the effective critical resolved shear stress. This behavior aligns with the expected strain‑rate‑dependent strengthening mechanisms in high‑entropy refractory systems, where the combination of solid‑solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and the lack of easy slip systems collectively raise the flow stress during high‑rate loading, as confirmed by the load‑dependent microhardness data.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Vacuum induction melting of the TiWVReTa refractory high‑entropy alloy was performed in a 3 kW induction furnace equipped with a water‑cooled copper crucible and a 5 mm diameter quartz tube to maintain a residual gas pressure below 1 × 10⁻⁵ Pa. Charge stoichiometry was achieved by weighing elemental Ti, W, V, Re, and Ta in a 1:1:1:1:1 ratio, followed by multiple melt–turn cycles to ensure homogeneity; the molten pool was tapped into a pre‑heated titanium mold, yielding a fully dense ingot with negligible porosity. For oxidation studies, disc specimens (≈ 5 mm diameter, 0.5 mm thick) were extracted from the central region and exposed in a horizontal tube furnace under flowing dry air at temperatures ranging from 800 °C to 1200 °C for durations up to 100 h. Weight gain data revealed a pronounced activation energy for the initial oxidation stage, after which the oxide scale evolved from a thin, adherent TiO₂ layer to a spalled, Re‑rich secondary phase rich in V₂O₅ and WO₃. Cross‑sectional scanning electron microscopy showed progressive coarsening of the oxide grains and a gradual increase in scale porosity, correlating with a transition from diffusion‑controlled growth to stress‑driven spallation. The presence of Re appeared to stabilize the oxide network, delaying the onset of scale delamination, whereas Ti and W contributed to the formation of a protective, continuous TiO₂ film at the lower end of the temperature range. processing_route: vacuum induction melting

text: During the arc‑melting of CrReTaWHf, the rapid solidification of the melt leads to a fine, largely austenitic microstructure with a high degree of lattice distortion due to the five-element mixture. Subsequent drop casting imposes a further cooling rate that preserves this fine structure, yet introduces a modest amount of porosity and residual stresses. When the alloy is annealed at temperatures near its recrystallization point, the high lattice parameter mismatch promotes a strong driving force for nucleation of new, strain‑free grains. Consequently, the recrystallized grains emerge with a markedly smaller size compared to the as‑cast microstructure, enhancing the overall strength through a refined grain size effect. However, because the constituent elements possess different melting points and diffusivities, the grain growth rate during prolonged annealing is initially suppressed, then accelerates once a critical grain size is reached. This two‑stage kinetic behavior results in a pronounced plateau in the grain size versus time curve, after which the growth rate follows a typical parabolic law. The combination of rapid nucleation and delayed coarsening yields a stable microstructure that retains high strength while limiting excessive grain enlargement.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloys TiTaNbZrMoHfW and ZrTaHfTiMoRe were synthesized by vacuum induction melting and characterized for notch sensitivity and fracture toughness in the brittle BCC regime. Both systems exhibit high lattice distortion and strong solid‑solution strengthening, yet the TiTaNbZrMoHfW alloy contains a higher proportion of Ti and Nb, which tend to form a more uniform, defect‑free matrix compared to the Re‑rich ZrTaHfTiMoRe alloy where Re segregation can produce localized softening zones. Consequently, the TiTaNbZrMoHfW alloy displays reduced notch sensitivity, as microcrack initiation is delayed by the homogeneous distribution of lattice distortion, leading to higher fracture toughness. In contrast, the Re‑containing alloy shows increased notch sensitivity due to Re‑induced compositional inhomogeneities that act as crack nucleation sites, thereby lowering its resistance to fracture under notched conditions.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The comparative hardness–yield strength assessment of the arc‑melted, drop‑cast refractory high‑entropy alloys ReVTaZrWHf and TiMoHfVW reveals a qualitative consistency with Tabor’s empirical relation. In both systems, the measured Vickers hardness is dominated by the fine, homogeneously distributed solid‑solution matrix, with only minor secondary phases such as Re‑rich intermetallics in the first alloy and Ti‑rich carbides in the second. The ReVTaZrWHf alloy, containing heavier elements with larger atomic radii and higher intrinsic shear modulus, exhibits a slightly higher lattice distortion and thus stronger solid‑solution hardening, leading to a modestly elevated hardness. Consequently, the yield strength of ReVTaZrWHf is expected to be higher than that of TiMoHfVW, following the Tabor‑type scaling that correlates yield strength to hardness. The TiMoHfVW alloy, while still hard due to Mo‑induced lattice distortion, experiences a relatively lower shear modulus and a slightly coarser grain structure from its processing, which collectively result in a somewhat reduced yield strength.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)

text: Vacuum induction melting of the NbW–Hf system was carried out under an Ar atmosphere, using a graphite crucible to minimize contamination. The ingot, cast in a 6‑mm diameter rod, was subsequently homogenized at 1800 °C for 24 h, followed by furnace cooling to 1200 °C and isothermal hold for 48 h to promote the dissolution of any primary β‑phase precipitates. Optical microscopy revealed a coarsened, equiaxed grain network in the as‑cast state, with an average grain size of ~25 µm, while the annealed sample exhibited a refined grain structure (~10 µm) due to recrystallization. Transmission electron microscopy identified a network of fine, body‑centered cubic (bcc) Nb‑rich lamellae, whose spacing decreased from ~150 nm in the as‑cast material to ~80 nm after heat treatment. This reduction in precipitate spacing, coupled with a more homogeneous distribution of Hf, is expected to enhance solid solution strengthening and suppress localized shear banding, thereby improving yield strength and ductility. The homogenized microstructure also exhibited a lower residual porosity fraction, as quantified by micro‑CT, indicating reduced internal stress concentrations.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The refractory high entropy alloy TiVTa was synthesized by arc melting of high purity elemental constituents followed by rapid drop casting into a copper mold. The rapid solidification inherent to the drop casting process suppresses the formation of equilibrium intermetallics, instead promoting the coexistence of a single body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution across the entire compositional range. X‑ray diffraction patterns show a single BCC reflection set with a lattice parameter intermediate to the constituent elements, confirming full solid solution formation. The absence of secondary phases is corroborated by transmission electron microscopy, which reveals a homogeneous microstructure with no discernible precipitates or ordered clusters. Thermodynamic calculations using the CALPHAD method predict a narrow two‑phase (BCC + BCC) miscibility gap at high temperatures, yet the rapid quench stabilizes the BCC phase down to ambient conditions. These findings suggest that the lattice distortion introduced by the size mismatch among Ti, V, and Ta, combined with high processing temperatures, favors the thermodynamic stability of a single BCC solid solution, which is a prerequisite for superior mechanical performance in refractory high‑entropy alloys.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy VZrCrTiNbMo, the large lattice distortion caused by the disparate atomic sizes of V, Zr, Cr, Ti, Nb, and Mo enhances the propensity for hydrogen solubility in the solid solution. During arc melting and subsequent drop casting, rapid solidification can trap hydrogen generated from trace moisture or surface oxidation into the matrix, creating supersaturated interstitial sites that promote the formation of brittle hydride‑like precipitates or localized stress fields. These hydrogen‑rich regions act as nucleation sites for cracking under tensile or cyclic loading, particularly when the alloy is cooled slowly enough for hydrides to grow. Furthermore, the high temperature processing can introduce micro‑porosity and residual stresses, which, combined with hydrogen embrittlement, reduce fracture toughness and elongation at fracture. Mitigating strategies such as de‑gas arc melting, vacuum drop casting, and post‑processing heat treatments at moderate temperatures help dissolve or redistribute hydrogen, thereby restoring ductility and improving overall mechanical performance.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc melting of the HfNbVTaZrW alloy was performed under high‑purity argon, using a water‑cooled copper crucible and a tungsten electrode to achieve rapid solidification. Multiple remelts ensured compositional homogeneity before the melt was dropped onto a pre‑heated steel plate to form a near‑dense ingot. Microstructural examination by scanning electron microscopy revealed a primarily single‑phase BCC matrix interspersed with fine, equiaxed secondary precipitates that nucleated preferentially along the solidification fronts. Energy‑dispersive X‑ray spectroscopy identified these inclusions as enriched in Hf and Zr, suggesting a metastable Hf–Zr rich phase. Nanoindentation hardness profiles showed a clear increase in hardness in regions with higher precipitate volume fraction, consistent with the obstacle‑to‑slip mechanism provided by the coherent precipitates. In contrast, areas where the secondary phase was coarsened or reduced exhibited a modest drop in hardness, underscoring the critical role of precipitate size and distribution in tuning the mechanical performance of this refractory HEA.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: In the NbZrTaCrWReTi high‑entropy alloy, the simultaneous incorporation of five refractory elements produces a highly distorted bcc lattice, which suppresses dislocation motion and confers resistance to high‑temperature deformation. Mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing homogenizes the constituent phases, yet the severe high‑energy milling can introduce a fine network of nanoscale carbides and intermetallic precipitates, particularly from Cr and Re, that act as potent sites for hydrogen uptake. During service in humid or aqueous environments, dissolved hydrogen can migrate to these defect sites, becoming trapped and forming localized TiH or ZrH phases. The resulting lattice expansion and stress concentration at the precipitate interfaces promote the nucleation of microvoids and the initiation of intergranular cracking, thereby lowering fracture toughness and elongation. Moreover, the high lattice distortion exacerbates the segregation of hydrogen to the grain boundaries, accelerating the embrittlement process. Consequently, the mechanical integrity of the alloy in hydrogen‑rich environments is governed by the density and distribution of nanoscale secondary phases and the associated hydrogen trapping mechanisms.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: VCrZrMoRe was fabricated by vacuum induction melting, followed by multiple remelts to ensure compositional homogeneity. Specimens were sealed in quartz ampoules under 10⁻⁶ mbar and melted at 2500 °C, then cast into copper chill molds to minimize thermal gradients. The cast ingots were sectioned and subjected to homogenization annealing at 2100 °C for 48 h under a flowing argon atmosphere to suppress constitutional segregation. After furnace cooling to room temperature, optical and scanning electron micrographs revealed a largely equiaxed structure with a mean grain size reduction relative to as-cast material. The high‑temperature treatment dissolved coarse intermetallic precipitates and redistributed the refractory elements, thereby diminishing local compositional spikes. Subsequent electron backscatter diffraction mapping showed a more uniform orientation distribution, confirming that homogenization reduced texture intensity and promoted a random grain orientation. The overall refinement of the microstructure is expected to enhance mechanical stability by mitigating strain‑localization pathways that would otherwise arise from the as‑cast compositional heterogeneity.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The refractory high entropy alloy VTaTi, fabricated by directed energy deposition, exhibits a complex interplay between its multi-component lattice and the rapid solidification inherent to laser additive manufacturing. The substantial atomic size mismatch among V, Ta, and Ti generates pronounced lattice distortion, which acts as a potent source of solid solution strengthening. During deposition, the extreme undercooling promotes the formation of a fine, homogeneous solid solution with minimal segregation, ensuring that the dislocation motion is impeded by the high local strain fields surrounding the larger Ta atoms and the smaller Ti atoms. Consequently, the yield strength increases monotonically with the relative concentration of Ta, as its larger radius amplifies the distortion field, while the inclusion of Ti, with its smaller radius, fine-tunes the lattice parameter and reduces the propensity for slip. Grain refinement induced by the rapid solidification further contributes to the yield strength, though its effect is secondary to the dominant solid solution mechanism in this system.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: In comparing the suction‑cast refractory high entropy alloys MoWVCrZr and ReWCrHf, both fabricated in a high‑purity argon environment, the work‑hardening response during tensile testing is governed by their distinct lattice distortion and solute distributions. MoWVCrZr, containing lighter transition metals with a relatively close atomic size match, exhibits a more coherent solid solution where dislocation motion is impeded by a moderate lattice strain. This leads to a modest initial hardening rate that gradually saturates as the microstructure evolves toward a stable fine‑grained phase. Conversely, ReWCrHf incorporates the heavy rhenium and hafnium, producing a pronounced lattice distortion and a higher density of substitutional solutes. The resulting solute‑drag effect and enhanced solute‑strengthening contribution sustain a steeper hardening trajectory over a broader strain interval, yielding a higher overall work‑hardening capacity. Therefore, ReWCrHf is expected to display a more pronounced work‑hardening behavior than MoWVCrZr during tensile deformation.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: High‑entropy alloys ReHfTa and HfCrMoTiV were fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering, producing dense microstructures with sub‑micron grains. In both systems, the Hall‑Petch relationship dominates, linking refined grain size to elevated yield strength and hardness. The ReHfTa alloy, containing the heavy, large‑radius element Re, exhibits slightly finer grains due to the strong solid‑solution strengthening that retards grain growth during sintering. Consequently, ReHfTa is expected to display higher hardness and yield strength compared to HfCrMoTiV, whose constituent elements (Cr, Mo, Ti, V) promote a marginally coarser grain structure as a result of more facile grain boundary migration. The greater lattice distortion and higher atomic‑size mismatch in ReHfTa further impede dislocation motion, reinforcing the strength advantage. Thus, the microstructural differences between the two alloys predict a systematic trend of increased hardness and strength for ReHfTa relative to HfCrMoTiV.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: In comparing the refractory high‑entropy alloys MoNbHfReWTi and NbTaReCrTi, both consolidated by powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering, the temperature dependence of tensile and yield strength reflects the relative contributions of solid‑solution hardening, lattice distortion, and secondary‑phase stability. MoNbHfReWTi incorporates heavier transition metals with a larger atomic radius mismatch, generating a pronounced lattice distortion that impedes dislocation glide even at elevated temperatures; this distortion is largely preserved through the sintered microstructure, yielding a relatively flat strength‑temperature curve. By contrast, NbTaReCrTi contains a greater proportion of early transition metals with smaller radius differences, resulting in less lattice distortion but stronger intermetallic precipitates that coarsen more rapidly as temperature rises. Consequently, the MoNbHfReWTi alloy tends to maintain higher yield and tensile strength at intermediate to high service temperatures, whereas NbTaReCrTi shows a more marked decline in strength with increasing temperature due to the accelerated loss of precipitate‑strengthening mechanisms and increased lattice diffusivity.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Mechanical alloying of Re, Hf, and W powders followed by hot‑pressing to 1.6 GPa at 1600 °C produced a dense, equiatomic ReHfW high‑entropy alloy with an average grain size of 15 µm and a uniform solid solution microstructure. Post‑processing annealing at 1400 °C for 2 h promoted the segregation of a minor HfO₂ phase along grain boundaries, providing a continuous oxide layer when the alloy was exposed to 900 °C in air. Thermogravimetric analysis revealed an initial weight gain that plateaued after ~30 min, indicating the formation of a passivating oxide skin. X‑ray diffraction of the oxidized surface identified Re₂O₇ and HfO₂ with a slight enrichment of W, suggesting that tungsten acts as a diffusion barrier for oxygen, slowing the growth of the oxide film. The resulting ReHfW exhibits superior oxidation resistance compared to binary W or Re alloys, attributable to the synergistic effect of the refractory elements and the finely distributed secondary oxides that limit oxygen permeation.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: Samples of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbZrVTiW were fabricated by arc melting each constituent element (≥99.5 % purity) in a water‑cooled copper hearth under a high‑purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted ten times with intermediate flipping to ensure homogeneity, after which it was cooled to room temperature before being extracted and sealed in a quartz ampoule. For drop‑casting, the molten alloy was poured onto a pre‑heated stainless‑steel mold at 2000 °C, then rapidly solidified over a 5 mm thick copper plate. Optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy‑dispersive X‑ray spectroscopy (EDS) revealed the formation of coherent Laves‑phase intermetallics, predominantly NbZr₂ and NbV₂, interspersed within a solid solution matrix. These precipitates preferentially nucleated at high‑energy sites such as grain boundaries and triple junctions, with typical interparticle spacings of 50–80 nm. X‑ray diffraction patterns showed distinct peaks corresponding to the C14 and C15 Laves structures, confirming their crystallographic stability at the casting temperature. The resulting microstructure, characterized by a fine dispersion of hard intermetallics in a ductile matrix, suggests enhanced solid‑solution strengthening and potential improvements in high‑temperature strength, while the residual porosity introduced during drop casting may act as a source of reduced toughness.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: secondary phase precipitation (Laves phases, intermetallics)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powders of Zr, Re, Hf, V, Ti, and Mo were blended in stoichiometric ratios and milled in a high‑energy ball‑milling system for 30 h under argon, yielding a homogeneous nanocrystalline mixture with an average grain size below 50 nm. The milled powders were uniaxially hot‑pressed at 1700 °C for 5 min under 50 MPa in a graphite die, producing dense compacts with porosity less than 1 %. Oxidation tests were conducted in a tube furnace under 5 % O₂/Ar at 900–1300 °C for up to 100 h. Mass gain data revealed a pronounced decrease in oxidation rate above 1100 °C, attributable to the formation of a protective mixed metal oxide layer rich in ZrO₂ and HfO₂. SEM/EDS mapping indicated a continuous, adherent oxide scale, while XRD confirmed the presence of monoclinic ZrO₂ and orthorhombic HfO₂ phases. The alloy’s high Re content contributed to the stability of the oxide network, suppressing spallation and maintaining low oxidation kinetics throughout the test window.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaHfCrMoTiWZr followed by hot pressing yielded a dense polycrystalline microstructure dominated by a single body‑centered cubic (bcc) solid solution with minor secondary intermetallics (e.g., HfMoTi‑type). The fracture toughness of this material exhibits a positive correlation with the volume fraction of the bcc phase: a higher bcc content promotes ductile crack initiation and deflection along coherent grain boundaries, whereas intermetallic inclusions act as stress concentrators. Grain boundary character analysis revealed a predominance of high‑angle boundaries, which enhance crack arrest by providing numerous barrier sites and promoting micro‑branching. When crack propagation encounters a secondary phase, the mismatch in lattice parameters and modulus generates local stress fields that encourage crack bending into the surrounding matrix, thereby increasing the energy required for catastrophic failure. Consequently, samples with finer bcc grains and a reduced intermetallic content display the highest fracture toughness, underscoring the importance of controlling phase distribution and boundary engineering in TaHfCrMoTiWZr alloys.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high entropy alloy WTaReZrNbMo followed by hot pressing results in a dense, single‑phase solid solution that is stabilized by thermodynamic factors. The calculated mixing enthalpy for this system is close to zero, indicating an almost ideal mixing of the constituent elements and a negligible tendency for intermetallic phase formation. The valence electron concentration (VEC) of the alloy lies near 5.6, a value that places it in the regime of body‑centered cubic stability at high temperature while still promoting a slight preference for a hexagonal close‑packed lattice at room temperature. This near‑isotropic electronic structure reduces the driving force for directional ordering, thereby enhancing the uniformity of the microstructure. Consequently, the alloy exhibits a narrow compositional window where solid solution strengthening dominates, with minimal precipitation or segregation that could otherwise compromise the mechanical integrity of the material.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrHfZrMoNb was carried out in a sealed argon atmosphere to suppress premature oxidation during solidification. The resulting ingot displayed a fine, nearly equiaxed microstructure with limited porosity, as confirmed by optical microscopy. Upon exposure to temperatures above 1200 °C in an air environment, the alloy formed a continuous, self‑limited oxide layer composed predominantly of Cr₂O₃, ZrO₂, and MoO₃ species, while the Hf and Nb constituents contributed to the stabilization of the oxide network through the formation of mixed oxides. Grain boundary diffusion of Cr and Zr facilitated the rapid outward transport of oxygen, leading to a gradual thickening of the protective scale over several hundred hours of isothermal testing. The high lattice distortion inherent to the CrHfZrMoNb composition promoted sluggish diffusion kinetics, thereby enhancing the barrier effectiveness of the oxide scale and preserving underlying metallic integrity at elevated temperatures.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: In laser‑directed energy deposition, the elastic response of refractory high‑entropy alloys is governed by the underlying crystal lattice and the bonding characteristics of the constituent elements. The HfReWTiTa alloy incorporates the heavy transition metal Re, which contributes a significant d‑band contribution and a more delocalized metallic bonding network; this tends to stiffen the lattice, raising the Young’s modulus relative to a system lacking such an element. Conversely, VHfTaNb contains V, whose larger atomic radius and more localized d‑electrons introduce a softer bonding character, while the Nb and Hf contribute to a relatively softer lattice when compared to Re. The combination of Ti and Ta in HfReWTiTa also promotes a more densely packed, high‑symmetry bcc or hcp structure with stronger metal–metal bonds, further elevating its modulus. Thus, one would expect HfReWTiTa to exhibit a higher elastic modulus than VHfTaNb, primarily due to the presence of Re and the resulting stronger metallic bonding and reduced lattice distortion.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition
