text: Powder‑metallurgy synthesis followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) produces a dense, near‑equiatomic WReCrVZr alloy with a single solid solution matrix and trace secondary precipitates of V‑rich carbides. Microstructural examination reveals that the average grain size remains fine (≈5 µm) across the processed specimens, yet the hardness varies markedly with the relative content of the secondary phase. When the V‑rich precipitates are suppressed—by adjusting the sintering temperature upward or by adding a small excess of Zr—the alloy displays a moderate hardness plateau, reflecting predominantly solid‑solution strengthening from the lattice distortion induced by the large atomic radii disparity. Conversely, increasing the V content or lowering the SPS temperature promotes the nucleation of fine V‑rich carbides; these coherent inclusions impede dislocation motion, producing a pronounced hardening effect that outpaces the modest grain‑size contribution. Thus, in WReCrVZr, the qualitative hardness trend is governed mainly by the fraction and coherency of the secondary V‑rich phase rather than by changes in the primary matrix or grain size.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In the TiZrReHf alloy series, arc melting and subsequent drop casting produced a dense, equiaxed microstructure with occasional intermetallic precipitates. Hardness measurements revealed that compositions with higher Re content exhibited a gradual increase in Vickers hardness, which can be attributed to the pronounced lattice distortion introduced by the heavy Re atom and its tendency to form fine TiRe and ZrRe intermetallics that act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion. Conversely, samples enriched in Ti and Zr tended to show a modest reduction in hardness, correlating with a lower density of secondary phases and a more homogeneous solid solution. The presence of discrete Hf-rich precipitates near the grain boundaries was also noted; these precipitates coarsened with increasing Hf fraction, leading to a slight softening effect due to reduced precipitation strengthening. Overall, the hardness trend across the TiZrReHf series underscores the critical role of secondary phase content and distribution in governing the mechanical response of this refractory high entropy alloy.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: Powder‐metallurgy synthesis followed by spark plasma sintering produced dense specimens of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrVWReHfMoTi, with an average porosity below 0.5 %. Three‑point‑bend fracture toughness tests conducted in accordance with ASTM E399/E1820 revealed a pronounced temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength. At room temperature the alloy exhibited a high yield plateau, attributed to the combined lattice distortion of the five transition metals and the fine‑grained microstructure (average grain size ~5 µm) which restricts dislocation motion. As the testing temperature was increased to 800 °C, the tensile strength dropped markedly while the yield strength remained comparatively robust, reflecting the activation of slip systems in the body‑centered cubic matrix and the reduced efficacy of solid‑solution strengthening at elevated temperatures. Beyond 900 °C both strengths declined rapidly, coincident with the appearance of localized softening and the formation of intermetallic secondary phases along grain boundaries, as indicated by electron probe microanalysis. These observations underscore the critical role of microstructural stability and phase evolution in governing the high‑temperature mechanical performance of ZrVWReHfMoTi.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high entropy alloy NbTaCrMoWReV was performed in a planetary mill under argon atmosphere, with 5 wt % Y₂O₃ added to suppress oxidation. 20 h of milling at 400 rpm produced a homogeneous nanocrystalline powder, evidenced by X‑ray diffraction peak broadening corresponding to an average grain size below 20 nm.  The high atomic size mismatch among Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W, Re, and V introduces substantial lattice distortion, which was quantified from the full‑width‑at‑half‑maximum of the (110) reflection; the distortion parameter exceeded 6 %.  Hot‑pressing at 1900 °C under 50 MPa for 2 h yielded fully dense compacts with porosity less than 0.5 %.  Microstructural analysis revealed a solid solution matrix with occasional nanometer‑scale secondary Cr‑rich clusters, while the pronounced lattice strain inhibited dislocation glide, leading to elevated hardness and yield strength.  The retained nanograin structure further reinforced these strengthening mechanisms, demonstrating the synergistic role of atomic size mismatch and processing‑induced grain refinement.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powders of Mo, Re, Ti, and Ta were mixed by high-energy ball milling for 12 h under argon, then sieved to 45–63 µm to ensure uniform particle size. The milled blend was uniaxially pressed at 300 MPa into cylindrical pellets and subjected to spark plasma sintering (SPS) in a graphite die: 1800 °C under a 60 MPa uniaxial load, with a heating rate of 100 °C min⁻¹ and a hold time of 10 min. Cooling was controlled at 200 °C min⁻¹ to 1200 °C, then furnace cooled to room temperature. Optical microscopy of polished cross‑sections revealed a largely equiaxed microstructure with an average grain size of ~15 µm, but occasional lamellar dendritic structures persisted at grain boundaries, particularly where Re-rich dendrites had coarsened during the high-temperature dwell. Energy‑dispersive X‑ray analysis showed segregation of Re to the interdendritic regions, resulting in a local lattice distortion that is expected to enhance solid‑solution strengthening, while the finer, equiaxed grains contribute to improved hardness and yield strength relative to coarser counterparts.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TiZrWCr produced a largely single‑phase body‑centered cubic (BCC) microstructure across a broad compositional window, as confirmed by X‑ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy. The lattice parameters were observed to vary monotonically with the overall Ti/Zr/W/Cr ratio, reflecting the substantial size mismatch among the constituent elements and the resultant lattice distortion. This distortion suppresses the formation of low‑temperature intermetallic phases that would otherwise emerge in binary Ti–Zr or Cr–W systems, thereby stabilizing the BCC solid solution down to room temperature. Scanning electron microscopy revealed a homogeneous distribution of Ti and Zr atoms within the BCC matrix, with only occasional, highly dispersed W‑rich nanoscale precipitates that are too sparse to alter the long‑range order. Consequently, the alloy exhibits a high degree of chemical homogeneity, and the BCC lattice remains metastable against the hexagonal close‑packed or orthorhombic phases that are often favored in refractory systems. These microstructural features underscore the pivotal role of multicomponent solid‑solution strengthening and lattice distortion in maintaining phase stability in TiZrWCr.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: The NbCrReTaV alloy synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing exhibits a pronounced yield strength enhancement attributable to extensive solid‑solution effects. During alloying, rapid bombardment of the constituent powders generates a highly disordered solid solution with significant lattice distortion, as Nb, Cr, Re, Ta, and V occupy the bcc lattice at comparable atomic sizes yet with varying valence electron counts. This distortion creates a high density of short‑range ordered clusters, which impede dislocation motion and elevate the critical resolved shear stress needed for plastic flow. Hot pressing at temperatures above the recrystallization range locks in fine equiaxed grains, further increasing yield strength via grain‑boundary strengthening. The combination of strong lattice strain fields from the multi‑principal elements and refined grain structure results in a monotonic increase in yield strength across the alloy’s compositional space, with higher Cr and V content amplifying the solid‑solution contribution due to their larger size and higher shear modulus.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WHfZr, synthesized by mixing equiatomic powders of W, Hf, and Zr followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at temperatures near 1600 °C, exhibits an elastic modulus that reflects the strong covalent‑metallic bonding of its constituent elements. In compression tests, the elastic response is governed by the combined lattice stiffness of the bcc‑derived solid solution and the interatomic distances set by the large atomic radii of Hf and Zr. Because W has the highest shear modulus among the three, the overall Young’s modulus increases with W content, while the inclusion of Hf and Zr introduces lattice distortion that slightly softens the elastic response but preserves a high modulus relative to conventional alloys. The observed yield points in compression are lower for samples with finer powder particles or higher SPS temperatures, indicating that grain refinement and reduced porosity diminish the brittle‑like yield behavior. Thus, elastic modulus trends in WHfZr are primarily dictated by the bonding character of the high‑atomic‑number refractory elements and the microstructural control afforded by powder metallurgy and SPS.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) produced a dense VHfNbTaCrW alloy with an equimolar composition and a predominantly body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix. During SPS, the rapid heating and short dwell times preserved a fine, nanocrystalline microstructure with grain sizes on the order of a few hundred nanometers, as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy. This high grain‑boundary density contributes to yield strength via the Hall–Petch mechanism, but the dominant strengthening factor in this system is solid‑solution interaction. The large atomic size mismatches among V, Hf, Nb, Ta, Cr, and W introduce significant lattice distortion, increasing the energy barriers for dislocation motion. As the alloy is cooled from the sintering temperature, the high solid‑solution strength manifests as a pronounced resistance to slip, thereby elevating the yield stress relative to binary or ternary counterparts. The presence of minor secondary phases, such as trace intermetallics at the grain boundaries, further impedes dislocation glide, reinforcing the observed yield behavior. Overall, the alloy demonstrates a marked rise in yield strength attributable to the combined effects of severe lattice distortion and fine‑grain solid‑solution strengthening.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: Vacuum induction melting of the TiHfRe alloy produced a coarse, nearly equiaxed structure composed of a single β‑phase matrix with minor Ti‑rich inclusions. Subsequent annealing at 1400 °C for 24 h under argon promoted extensive diffusion, reducing compositional segregation and dissolving the Ti‑rich particles. The homogenized microstructure exhibited a finer, more uniform grain size compared to the as‑cast state, with average equiaxed grains of ~15 µm. This grain refinement is associated with a higher yield strength, as the increased grain boundary area impedes dislocation motion. In addition, the dissolution of secondary Ti‑rich phases eliminated local stress concentrators, thereby improving fracture toughness and reducing the tendency for intergranular cracking. The homogenized alloy also displayed a more homogeneous lattice distortion, enhancing solid solution strengthening while minimizing porosity. Consequently, the annealed TiHfRe shows a balanced improvement in mechanical performance, with higher strength and toughness relative to the as‑cast material.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: Mechanical alloying followed by hot‑pressing produces dense, nanocrystalline refractory high‑entropy alloys such as CrWMoVHfTa and ReCrMoTiV, yet their compressive yield behavior diverges because of distinct microstructural features. In CrWMoVHfTa the broad solid‑solution strengthening from the five‑element mixture generates a highly distorted lattice that suppresses dislocation glide in both tension and compression, while the relatively coarse, intergranular Ti‑rich precipitates formed during sintering provide additional barrier to strain localization in compression. Consequently, the compressive yield strength of CrWMoVHfTa is only slightly lower than its tensile counterpart, reflecting a modest asymmetry. By contrast, ReCrMoTiV contains a higher proportion of Re, which promotes finer grain refinement through solid‑solution effects and induces a higher degree of lattice strain. However, Re also stabilizes a body‑centered cubic (BCC) phase that is intrinsically more susceptible to shear‐band initiation under compression, leading to a larger tensile‑compressive yield contrast. Thus, ReCrMoTiV is expected to exhibit a more pronounced asymmetry, with compressive yield strength appreciably lower than its tensile yield strength, whereas CrWMoVHfTa would show a smaller difference between the two modes.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: Mechanical alloying of the TaTiVZrNbHfW refractory high‑entropy alloy was conducted in a high‑energy planetary mill using a 10:1 ball‑to‑powder ratio under argon, producing a uniform fine‑grained powder with an average particle size of ~10 µm after 15 h. The milled powder was compacted by hot pressing at 1700 °C for 30 min in a vacuum furnace, yielding dense ingots with a relative density above 99 %. To evaluate anisotropic tensile behavior, specimens were machined from both the hot‑pressed ingots and from additively manufactured (laser‑directed energy deposition) builds that exhibit pronounced columnar texture along the build direction. Tensile tests performed along and transverse to the build axis revealed that the textured samples show higher yield and ultimate strengths when loaded parallel to the columnar grains, attributable to grain boundary alignment and enhanced solid‑solution strengthening along the preferred crystallographic orientations. Transverse loading, however, produced lower strengths and reduced elongation, reflecting increased grain boundary sliding and a higher prevalence of intergranular porosity. These observations confirm that the directional microstructure imposed by additive manufacturing strongly influences the mechanical anisotropy of the TaTiVZrNbHfW alloy.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser‑directed energy deposition of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrTiW creates a fully dense, columnar‑grain microstructure oriented along the build direction. In this BCC‑dominated system, the lattice distortion from the large atomic size mismatch of Zr, Ti, and W generates a substantial solid‑solution strengthening field, while the high melting temperatures preserve a narrow solidification band that limits the formation of coarse secondary phases. When evaluated by ASTM E399/E1820 three‑point‑bend specimens, the measured fracture toughness is markedly lower than that of ductile refractory HEAs, reflecting the inherent brittleness of the BCC matrix at room temperature. Notch sensitivity is pronounced: the presence of a 0.5 mm pre‑crack amplifies stress intensity such that the critical energy release rate drops to only a few times the baseline value. Micro‑damage analysis shows rapid initiation of microcracks at grain boundary junctions, where the high lattice strain concentrates stress. Consequently, fracture toughness correlates inversely with the degree of notch sensitivity; reducing crack length by controlling residual stresses through post‑processing heat treatment or adjusting scan strategy can mitigate the sensitivity and modestly enhance the toughness.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Vacuum‑induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VTaTiCrHf yields a nearly single‑phase solid solution with a body‑centered cubic lattice. The compositional homogeneity and absence of deleterious intermetallics are confirmed by electron backscatter diffraction, revealing a fine equiaxed grain population with an average size below 5 µm. Such grain refinement contributes to a higher propensity for dislocation nucleation and cross‑slip, thereby enhancing ductility. The pronounced lattice distortion from the wide spread of atomic radii among V, Ta, Ti, Cr, and Hf generates significant solid‑solution strengthening but also facilitates localized plasticity by enabling multiple slip systems to be activated at moderate stresses. However, the relatively high Cr content promotes the formation of nanometer‑sized Cr‑rich second phases at grain boundaries, which can act as crack nucleation sites under tensile loading, limiting the overall elongation at fracture. Controlling the melt cooling rate and performing post‑solidification annealing to dissolve or homogenize these boundary phases can further improve ductility by reducing internal stress concentrations and maintaining a uniform, high‑strength matrix.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: Arc‑melted and drop‑cast WVZrMoTa ingots were homogenized at elevated temperature to explore the evolution of a single‑phase body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution. During initial rapid solidification, compositional segregation manifested as Zr‑rich lamellae and Mo‑rich intergrowths, producing an anisotropic grain network. Subsequent isothermal annealing at 1700 °C for 48 h induced extensive interdiffusion, eliminating most compositional gradients and yielding a markedly more equiaxed microstructure with average grain size reduced by approximately 40 %. The homogenization also suppressed the formation of intermetallic second phases, as evidenced by the disappearance of the weakly scattering precipitates seen in as‑cast diffraction patterns. These microstructural refinements were accompanied by a shift toward a uniform lattice distortion profile, enhancing solid‑solution strengthening and thereby increasing the alloy’s yield strength while preserving ductility. The study demonstrates that controlled annealing can tailor the grain architecture and compositional homogeneity of WVZrMoTa, directly influencing its mechanical performance.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReHfVTaZrMoNb was carried out at 1900 °C under 10⁻⁵ mbar, followed by rapid quenching to retain a supersaturated solid solution. Subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C for 48 h produced a duplex microstructure comprising a body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix and a minor hexagonal close‑packed (HCP) intermetallic phase enriched in Re and Hf. Optical microscopy revealed average grain sizes of 30–40 µm for the BCC phase and 10–15 µm for the HCP phase. Nanoindentation mapping across a 200 µm × 200 µm region showed local hardness peaks of 20–22 GPa in the HCP precipitates and 18–19 GPa in the BCC matrix, while reduced modulus values of 400–420 GPa and 410–430 GPa were recorded respectively, indicating a slight compliance in the intermetallics. Tensile tests performed at room temperature on 5 mm gauge‑length samples indicated that specimens with finer BCC grains (≈20 µm) exhibited higher ultimate tensile strength compared to those with coarser grains (≈50 µm), consistent with a grain‑size‑strengthening trend. Moreover, the presence of Re‑rich HCP phase contributed to a modest increase in yield strength through solid‑solution and precipitation hardening, yet the overall ductility decreased due to the brittle nature of the secondary phase. These observations suggest that tailoring the Re:Hf ratio to control the volume fraction and size of the HCP intermetallics, alongside grain refinement of the BCC matrix, can balance strength and toughness in this refractory HEA system.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: qualitative tensile strength trends relative to composition and grain size
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes were employed to fabricate VWHfTiCrMoTa and TiVHfZrMo, each consolidated by spark plasma sintering at 1800 °C under 60 MPa for 5 min, yielding near‑full density compacts with fine equiaxed grains. Compression tests on cylindrical specimens revealed that VWHfTiCrMoTa exhibited a pronounced asymmetry relative to its tensile counterpart: the compressive yield stress was markedly higher, reflecting the enhanced resistance of the bcc lattice to densification and the stabilizing influence of the high‑entropy solid solution formed by V, W, Hf, Ti, Cr, Mo, and Ta. In contrast, TiVHfZrMo displayed a smaller yield asymmetry, with compressive yield stress only modestly exceeding its tensile yield. This difference is attributed to the partial substitution of Zr, which promotes the formation of nanoscale intergranular TiH phases, softening the compressive response. Consequently, VWHfTiCrMoTa is expected to trend higher in compressive yield strength due to its more coherent solid solution and reduced susceptibility to intergranular weakening.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy Ta₃₀W₂₀Nb₂₀Hf₁₀Ti₂₀ under an argon atmosphere produced a near‑single‑phase β‑solid solution with fine equiaxed grains. Hardness mapping revealed a clear correlation with the volume fraction of Ti‑rich secondary intermetallics that precipitate along grain boundaries. Samples with a modest 5–8 % Ti‑rich phase exhibited the highest Vickers hardness, attributable to coherent precipitates that impede dislocation motion through Orowan looping. As Ti content increased beyond 12 %, the secondary phase grew into a percolating network, causing grain boundary embrittlement and a reduction in hardness due to increased grain boundary sliding. Conversely, reducing Ti to below 3 % minimized secondary phase formation but also reduced lattice distortion, leading to a softer alloy. Thus, the hardness of TaWNbHfTi can be tuned by balancing Ti‑driven secondary phase precipitation against maintaining a coherent, dense β matrix.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: Suction‑cast specimens of TiNbReZr and CrZrRe, fabricated under a high‑purity argon shield, exhibit distinct compressive yield responses that reflect their contrasting lattice and phase architectures. TiNbReZr, characterized by a homogeneous bcc solid solution with minor Ti–Zr interstitials, displays a pronounced asymmetry: its compressive yield strength is appreciably higher than the tensile counterpart due to the enhanced resistance of the bcc lattice to dislocation glide under compression, combined with a reduced propensity for twinning that otherwise weakens tension. In contrast, CrZrRe, which incorporates a mixture of bcc and metastable hcp regions arising from rapid solidification, shows a more symmetric stress–strain curve; the hcp interphase facilitates cross‑slip and twin nucleation, mitigating the yield asymmetry. Consequently, TiNbReZr is expected to trend toward a higher compressive yield strength relative to CrZrRe, driven by its more uniform lattice distortion and lower secondary‑phase content that limits localized strain accommodation.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: In the present investigation the refractory high‑entropy alloy HfWReNbCr was synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing to produce dense, fully bonded samples suitable for tensile testing. The powder blending yielded a homogenous solid solution with minor secondary HfCr‐rich phases confined to grain boundaries. Hot pressing at 1800 °C and 20 MPa produced a columnar microstructure with pronounced c‑axis texture, as confirmed by X‑ray diffraction pole figures. When tensile specimens were cut parallel and perpendicular to the build direction, the parallel orientation exhibited higher ultimate tensile and yield strengths, attributable to alignment of the hexagonal close‑packed lattice along the load direction and to the greater density of high‑angle grain boundaries that impede dislocation glide. Conversely, the perpendicular orientation displayed increased ductility, reflecting the ability of twinning and slip on the basal plane to accommodate strain. These directional dependencies underscore the critical role of processing‑induced texture in tailoring the mechanical response of HfWReNbCr high‑entropy alloys.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: In comparing the fracture toughness of the suction‑cast refractory high‑entropy alloys CrTiMoWTaVHf and HfTaVReW, the primary determinant is the evolution of their multiphase microstructures during rapid solidification under argon. CrTiMoWTaVHf, with its broader atomic size mismatch and a higher proportion of intermetallics such as Cr₂W and TiMo, tends to form a more complex, fine‑scale intergranular network that can deflect cracks and promote energy dissipation. The grain boundaries in this alloy often exhibit a higher fraction of high‑angle boundaries, which can accommodate localized plasticity and blunt propagating cracks, thereby enhancing fracture toughness. Conversely, HfTaVReW, while also solid‑solution–strengthened, develops a relatively coarser β‑phase matrix and fewer secondary intermetallic precipitates. Its grain boundaries are predominantly low‑angle, offering less resistance to crack initiation and less tortuous crack paths, resulting in a comparatively lower fracture toughness. Thus, CrTiMoWTaVHf would plausibly exhibit higher fracture toughness than HfTaVReW due to its richer phase content, finer grain size, and more favorable grain boundary character that collectively impede crack progression.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: In comparing VMoZrTiCrReNb and ZrNbMoReTi processed by powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering, the anisotropy of tensile response is largely governed by the degree of crystallographic texture imparted during additive manufacturing or directional solidification. The VMoZrTiCrReNb alloy, containing the larger V and Cr atoms, exhibits a higher lattice distortion that promotes pronounced columnar growth along the build direction; this texture aligns the Burgers vectors preferentially, leading to enhanced yield strength but reduced elongation perpendicular to the build axis. Conversely, the ZrNbMoReTi system, with a more homogeneous atomic size distribution and a smaller Ti contribution, develops a weaker texture, resulting in a more isotropic tensile response where the yield and ultimate strengths are slightly lower than in the VMoZrTiCrReNb alloy, yet the fracture toughness and ductility are comparatively higher across all orientations. Therefore, one would anticipate VMoZrTiCrReNb to trend higher in anisotropic strength, whereas ZrNbMoReTi would display a more balanced mechanical performance.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Arc melting followed by drop casting produces coarse, equiaxed microstructures in both CrMoZr and HfReZrTaWCrMo. During tensile deformation, work hardening is governed by the ability of dislocations to encounter obstacles such as lattice distortion, solid‑solution strengthening, and precipitate spacing. The CrMoZr alloy, composed of early transition metals with a relatively low atomic size mismatch, exhibits modest lattice distortion and a simpler solid‑solution matrix; dislocations can glide with fewer impediments, leading to a lower rate of work hardening and a more gradual increase in strength with strain. In contrast, HfReZrTaWCrMo contains high‑Z elements (Hf, Re, Ta, W) that introduce substantial atomic radius disparity, increasing lattice distortion and producing a higher density of solute atoms. These features act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion, enhancing strain‑hardening rate. Consequently, HfReZrTaWCrMo would plausibly display a steeper work‑hardening curve and reach a higher flow stress at comparable strains, while CrMoZr would harden more slowly.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: Laser additive manufacturing of refractory high‑entropy alloys NbCrReVTiMo and WTiNbReTaZr by directed energy deposition yields columnar microstructures aligned with the build direction. In both systems, the pronounced lattice distortion and high solid‑solution strength promote isotropic basal strengthening; however, the texture development during rapid solidification induces anisotropy in tensile response. NbCrReVTiMo, containing relatively low‑atomic‑number elements such as Cr and V, exhibits a weaker <111> texture and finer interdendritic regions, leading to a modest reduction of ultimate tensile strength along the build direction compared with the transverse direction. Conversely, WTiNbReTaZr, dominated by high‑atomic‑number refractory constituents, develops a strong <001> preferred orientation and more pronounced columnar grains, which enhance strength along the build axis but simultaneously increase the susceptibility to cleavage along basal planes, thereby reducing elongation at fracture in that orientation. Thus, while both alloys display anisotropic behavior, WTiNbReTaZr is expected to trend higher tensile strength along the build direction at the expense of ductility, whereas NbCrReVTiMo offers a more balanced but slightly lower strength–ductility combination.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloys NbVCr and HfTiCrV produces columnar grains that are largely texture‑free, yet the microstructural evolution during rapid solidification dictates their hardness. In NbVCr, the equiatomic mix of a transition metal (Nb), a group IVB metal (V), and a group V metal (Cr) generates a modest lattice distortion; however, the high cooling rate suppresses extensive precipitation, leaving the solid solution largely single‑phase body‑centered cubic. Consequently, hardness is governed primarily by solid‑solution strengthening and grain‑boundary strengthening, yielding a moderate value. By contrast, HfTiCrV, containing a large‑atomic‑radius Hf and a smaller Ti, induces greater lattice strain and promotes the formation of intermetallic secondary phases such as TiCr or HfCr compounds during solidification. These brittle intermetallic precipitates act as hard, dispersed obstacles to dislocation motion, enhancing hardness relative to NbVCr. Therefore, HfTiCrV would plausibly exhibit higher hardness than NbVCr due to its richer secondary‑phase content and increased lattice distortion.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: In the powder‑metallurgy route to the refractory high‑entropy alloy WTiHfCr, spark plasma sintering consolidates the nanoscale powders into a dense feedstock while preserving a fine equiaxed grain structure; this microstructure, combined with the large lattice distortion introduced by the four principal elements, sets the stage for pronounced strain‑rate sensitivity. Rockwell hardness measurements performed at progressively higher loading rates reveal a systematic increase in hardness, consistent with a strengthening mechanism that is highly dynamic: at low strain rates the sluggish diffusion of W, Ti, Hf, and Cr allows vacancy migration and grain boundary sliding to relax stresses, whereas at high strain rates the reduced time for such relaxation leads to a greater proportion of dislocation storage and forest hardening. Moreover, the high atomic‑size mismatch enhances short‑range order during sintering, creating nanoscale precipitates that act as efficient pinning points; their effectiveness is markedly higher when the material is strained rapidly, further amplifying the rate‑dependent hardness response. Thus, the measured Rockwell hardness trend underscores the interplay of solid‑solution strengthening, grain boundary strengthening, and precipitation hardening in dictating the strain‑rate sensitivity of WTiHfCr.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark‑plasma sintering produced equiaxed microstructures for both HfNbZrMoReCrW and NbVTi, yet the average grain size in the former remained roughly 1.2‑fold larger than that of the latter. This disparity can be attributed to the higher overall atomic size mismatch and the stronger tendency of HfNbZrMoReCrW to form sluggish diffusion phases, which retard grain boundary migration during the rapid sintering cycle. According to Hall‑Petch considerations, the reduced grain size in NbVTi yields a more pronounced grain‑boundary strengthening contribution, thereby elevating its hardness and yield strength relative to HfNbZrMoReCrW. Moreover, the lighter constituent elements in NbVTi promote a more coherent solid solution with fewer lattice distortions, further enhancing its resistance to dislocation glide. Consequently, NbVTi is expected to trend higher in both hardness and strength, whereas HfNbZrMoReCrW, with its coarser grains and higher lattice distortion, would exhibit comparatively lower values.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: MoZrTaVCr was fabricated by suction casting within an argon atmosphere to suppress initial oxidation. Upon exposure to 1000 °C in air, the alloy exhibited a self‑limited oxide layer composed primarily of ZrO₂ and Ta₂O₅, with minor Cr₂O₃ and MoO₃ contributions. The dense, adherent nature of the oxide barrier curtailed further diffusion of oxygen into the bulk, preserving the underlying microstructure. At temperatures approaching 1200 °C, the oxide scale grew in thickness and began to spall due to the mismatch in thermal expansion coefficients, which released stored strain energy. Despite spallation, the alloy’s high melting point and the presence of refractory elements mitigated rapid grain coarsening, maintaining fine grains (~5 µm) that contribute to strength retention. The formation of a continuous, protective ZrO₂ layer also reduced the susceptibility to oxidation‐induced embrittlement compared to alloys lacking a stable refractory oxide component.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReMoWVNbCrTa yielded a near‑equiatomic, single‑phase bcc solid solution with minimal porosity. Tensile specimens tested per ASTM E8 at room temperature reveal a pronounced ductility‑strength trade‑off characteristic of refractory HEAs: increasing alloying element concentration, which broadens the lattice parameter distribution and enhances solid‑solution hardening, simultaneously reduces the elongation at fracture. Micro‑fractography shows that the reduction in ductility arises from the nucleation of localized shear bands within the fine‑grained microstructure, where the high lattice distortion promotes early onset of plastic instability. Conversely, specimens annealed to promote grain growth exhibit modest increases in uniform elongation but at the expense of a slight decline in yield strength, underscoring the delicate balance between grain‑size‑controlled work hardening and lattice‑distortion‑driven strengthening mechanisms in ReMoWVNbCrTa.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: Suction casting of TaNbVReMoZr under an inert argon atmosphere yielded a nearly equiatomic body‑centred cubic (BCC) microstructure with uniformly distributed secondary Laves‑type intermetallics. Cyclic loading tests at room temperature revealed a pronounced fatigue‑strength envelope, where low‑cycle fatigue was dominated by intergranular cracking initiated at grain boundary junctions, while high‑cycle fatigue showed transgranular propagation governed by the high lattice distortion intrinsic to the alloy. The dense network of Laves phases acted as effective crack‑bridging obstacles, increasing crack‑growth resistance and extending the fatigue life beyond that expected from the alloy’s yield strength alone. Moreover, the observed grain refinement, with an average size of 3–4 µm, contributed to a reduced mean free path for dislocation motion, thereby raising the threshold stress intensity factor for crack initiation. Overall, the combination of solid‑solution strengthening, secondary phase dispersion, and fine grain size synergistically improved fatigue crack initiation resistance and slowed propagation, highlighting the role of microstructural engineering in enhancing the endurance of refractory high‑entropy alloys.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: The NbVWMoRe alloy, fabricated by suction casting in an argon‑purged environment, displays a predominantly body‑centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with a fine, equiaxed grain network. Vickers microhardness testing performed at multiple indentation sites reveals a modest spatial variability in hardness, reflecting subtle fluctuations in local grain size and minor segregation of Re along grain boundaries. Notch sensitivity, assessed through the ratio of notched to unnotched fracture toughness, increases as the indentation depth approaches the surface, indicating that localized hardening near the notch exacerbates stress concentration. The observed hardness gradient correlates with a reduced capacity for plastic dissipation at the notch root, leading to a higher propensity for crack initiation and propagation in this brittle BCC alloy. Consequently, the fracture toughness is markedly diminished in notched specimens, underscoring the importance of controlling grain refinement and eliminating Re‑rich boundary phases to mitigate notch sensitivity in NbVWMoRe high‑entropy systems.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: High‑entropy alloy HfMoWTaReZr was fabricated by ball‑millled powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering, achieving a dense microstructure with minimal porosity. Hot‑tensile tests performed up to 1 200 °C in a controlled‑atmosphere furnace revealed a pronounced increase in yield strength with temperature, indicative of significant solid‑solution hardening. The large atomic size mismatch among Hf, Mo, W, Ta, Re, and Zr induces pronounced lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation motion and elevates yield stresses even at elevated temperatures. Grain refinement observed in the sintered specimens further enhances the strength through the Hall–Petch mechanism. Moreover, the multi‑principal composition promotes the formation of a fine dispersion of nanoscale BCC–like secondary phases, which act as additional obstacles to dislocation glide. Together, these microstructural features explain the observed yield‑strength trends, underscoring the dominant role of solid‑solution strengthening in dictating the mechanical response of HfMoWTaReZr at high temperatures.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: Mechanical alloying of MoTiHfWTaCrNb generates a homogeneous supersaturated solid solution that, after hot pressing, undergoes rapid sintering and partial recrystallization. The resulting microstructure typically exhibits sub‑micron grains, with an average grain size of 0.5–1.0 µm, and minimal porosity due to the high‐pressure consolidation. In this refractory high‑entropy alloy, the Hall‑Petch relationship is evident: as the grain boundary area increases, dislocation motion is impeded, leading to higher flow stress and consequently elevated hardness. Finer grains also promote a higher density of strain‑gradient sources, which enhance the overall strength without severely compromising ductility. The pronounced lattice distortion from the large atomic size mismatch among Mo, Ti, Hf, W, Ta, Cr, and Nb contributes additional solid‑solution strengthening, but the primary driver for the observed increase in strength and hardness remains the refined grain structure. Thus, controlling the grain size during processing allows systematic tuning of the alloy’s mechanical performance.

text: During tensile loading of refractory high‑entropy alloys produced by directed energy deposition, the work‑hardening response is governed by the evolution of dislocation density, the interaction of lattice distortion, and the presence of secondary phases. In TaZrReWCrHf, the combination of large atomic size differences (Δr ≈ 0.14 Å) and the high fraction of refractory elements generates strong lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation motion and promotes a pronounced strain‑rate sensitivity. Consequently, the alloy exhibits a steep initial work‑hardening rate that gradually tapers as dynamic recovery becomes significant. By contrast, NbHfTaTi contains a smaller spread of atomic sizes (Δr ≈ 0.10 Å) and a more homogeneous solid‑solution matrix. Its lower lattice distortion leads to less dislocation pile‑up and a more modest hardening slope. Moreover, the Nb–Hf pairing stabilizes a fine, coherent BCC/NbTi‑like subphase that facilitates easier cross‑slip, further reducing work hardening. Thus, TaZrReWCrHf would plausibly display a higher work‑hardening trend than NbHfTaTi during tensile deformation.

text: Powder metallurgy was employed to fabricate the ReZrWCrV alloy, with elemental powders mixed in equiatomic proportions and ball‑milled for 24 h to promote intimate mixing and reduce particle size to below 20 µm. The milled mixture was cold‑compacted at 600 MPa and subjected to spark plasma sintering at 1600 °C for 5 min under a pressure of 50 MPa, yielding near‑fully dense compacts. To probe the influence of a homogenization treatment, samples were annealed at 1400 °C for 10 h followed by furnace cooling. Optical and electron microscopy revealed that the as‑sintered microstructure contained fine, interlocked dendritic regions with a high density of incoherent secondary phases rich in Cr and V. Post‑annealing, the dendrites coarsened and the secondary phase distribution became more uniform, reducing local compositional gradients. The resulting microstructure exhibited a more homogeneous solid solution, with a reduction in residual stresses and a modest increase in grain size, suggesting that the homogenization treatment promotes phase equilibrium and potentially enhances ductility while preserving strength due to retained lattice distortion.

text: A 10‑g batch of NbWVCrTaMoZr was melted in a vacuum induction furnace under 10⁻⁵ Torr, using an argon atmosphere to avoid oxidation of V and Mo. The molten alloy was cast into a 10 mm diameter rod and homogenized at 1900 °C for 4 h before furnace cooling to 600 °C, then water quenched. Resulting microstructure revealed a single BCC solid solution with fine (<5 µm) equiaxed grains, minor carbides of Cr and V distributed at grain boundaries, and a slight porosity (<1 vol %). Compression tests on 5 mm × 5 mm coupons exhibited a higher yield stress than tension, with the compressive yield plateau occurring at 5–10 % greater load. This asymmetry is attributed to the BCC lattice’s higher resistance to dislocation nucleation under compressive shear, while tensile loading preferentially activates twinning and slip on {110} planes, leading to earlier yielding. The presence of finely spaced carbides further impedes dislocation motion under compression, enhancing the yield asymmetry.

text: During preparation of the refractory high‑entropy alloy V–W–Zr–Mo–Hf–Nb, a single‑piece ingot was fabricated by vacuum induction melting followed by multiple remelts to ensure chemical homogeneity; the alloy was subsequently forged and homogenized at temperatures approaching the melting point to promote complete solid solution formation. To protect the alloy’s surface during high‑temperature service, a dense, low‑porosity alumina‑based coating was deposited by high‑temperature plasma spraying. The coating, rich in Al₂O₃ and fine AlN secondary phases, adheres to the substrate through interfacial diffusion of Ti and Zr, which form a graded transition layer that mitigates thermal mismatch. In situ X‑ray diffraction revealed that the coating remains largely cubic Al₂O₃ up to 1400 °C, while the underlying alloy retains its body‑centred cubic lattice with only slight lattice distortion due to the high atomic radius disparity among V, W, Mo, Hf, and Nb. Mechanical testing demonstrated that the coating suppresses oxidation‑induced grain boundary sliding, preserving the high‑temperature strength of the HEA by limiting grain growth and maintaining a fine, equiaxed microstructure.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting

text: In the refractory high entropy alloy HfVReTiZrWTa, powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering yields a dense microstructure characterized by a fine equiaxed grain population and a relatively homogeneous solid solution of the constituent elements. During tensile deformation, the alloy exhibits pronounced work hardening, a consequence of the complex interplay between lattice distortion and the high density of dislocations that is amplified by the large atomic size differences among Hf, V, Re, Ti, Zr, W, and Ta. The Rockwell hardness measurements taken on partially deformed specimens reveal a steady increase in hardness with accumulated strain, reflecting the buildup of internal stresses and the activation of multiple slip systems. This hardening behavior is further reinforced by the sluggish diffusion kinetics intrinsic to refractory alloys, which suppress dynamic recovery and enable the retention of high dislocation densities. Consequently, the observed hardness trend correlates strongly with the alloy’s capacity to resist plastic deformation, highlighting the critical role of solid solution strengthening and microstructural stability in dictating its tensile work hardening response.

text: Suction casting of VTaTiZrMoRe was performed at 2000 °C in a sealed alumina crucible under flowing argon to suppress oxidation. A 12 mm diameter rod was melted for 30 s and then drawn into a 5 mm diameter rod through a 0.5 mm throat at a controlled feed rate, yielding a near‐equiaxed microstructure with average grain size around 10 µm and minimal porosity. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out on 4 mm gauge length specimens at strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹ at room temperature. Strength increased monotonically with strain rate, with the high‑rate specimens exhibiting a pronounced plateau in stress–strain curves, indicative of strain‑rate–induced phase transformations. Analysis of the microstructure after fracture revealed a higher density of sub‑grains and twins in the high‑rate tests, suggesting dynamic recovery processes are activated under rapid deformation, thereby elevating the apparent yield and ultimate strengths while slightly reducing elongation.

text: Vacuum‑induced melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaCrHfMoTi produced a dense ingot with minimal porosity, confirmed by optical inspection. The high‑temperature oxidation study, conducted between 1000 °C and 1400 °C in air, revealed a self‑limiting oxidation layer dominated by the formation of a protective chromia‑rich phase. As the temperature rises, the Cr and Ta constituents preferentially segregate to the surface, generating a compact Cr₂O₃ network that impedes oxygen diffusion. Concurrently, Mo and Ti contribute to the stability of the interfacial oxide by forming a mixed MoO₃/TiO₂ layer that adheres strongly to the underlying alloy. The lattice distortion inherent to the multi‑principal system reduces the diffusivity of oxygen through the bulk, further slowing weight gain. When the temperature exceeds 1300 °C, the protective coating begins to spall due to thermal stress, yet the underlying alloy continues to exhibit only modest mass increase, indicating a robust oxidation resistance that stems from the synergistic action of the constituent oxides and the alloy's solid‑solution matrix.

text: Laser‐directed energy deposition was used to fabricate near‐stoichiometric refractory high‑entropy alloys (HEAs) TaReVNbW and CrZrTiVHfTa, and their tensile response was examined at ambient temperature. Microstructural analysis revealed a columnar dendritic grain structure in both alloys, but TaReVNbW exhibited finer grains and a higher volume fraction of nanoscale coherent carbides, while CrZrTiVHfTa displayed coarser grains and a modest intermetallic network. During deformation, the TaReVNbW alloy demonstrates pronounced work‑hardening, attributable to the high lattice distortion from the wide range of atomic sizes and the impediment of dislocation motion by the dense secondary phase population. In contrast, CrZrTiVHfTa shows a more limited hardening rate, as the larger grains and less pronounced phase contrast allow easier dislocation glide. Consequently, TaReVNbW is expected to trend higher in work‑hardening capacity and maintain elevated flow stress at larger strains compared with CrZrTiVHfTa.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes followed by spark‑plasma sintering produced dense monolithic specimens of NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ and CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅, each exhibiting a near‑equiatomic composition apart from the minor alloying additions. Microstructural examinations revealed a fine equiaxed grain network for both alloys, yet the CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅ matrix contained a higher fraction of secondary W–Cr carbides precipitated during the sintering dwell, whereas the NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ microstructure was dominated by a single solid‑solution phase with slight Nb–Hf partitioning at grain boundaries. The compressive yield stress of CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅ exceeded that of NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅, a trend attributable to the additional solid‑solution hardening from Ta and the strengthening effect of the carbide inclusions, which impede dislocation glide under compressive loading. In contrast, tensile yield in both alloys displayed a more pronounced asymmetry; the NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ alloy showed a relatively lower tensile yield, likely due to its more uniform lattice distortion and absence of carbides, which reduces the ability of dislocations to nucleate and propagate in tension. Consequently, CrW₀.₇₅Ta₀.₂₅ is projected to exhibit a higher compressive yield strength, while tensile asymmetry favors the NbW₀.₇₅Hf₀.₂₅ alloy to display a lower tensile yield stress
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: In the present study, the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrHfWReNbZrTi was synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying followed by hot‑press sintering at 1800 °C under argon, yielding a dense microstructure with sub‑micrometer equiaxed grains and minimal porosity. Oxidation kinetics were evaluated in air from 1200 to 1600 °C for up to 500 h, revealing an initially rapid mass gain that transitions to a parabolic regime. The formation of a continuous Cr‑rich surface oxide layer, enriched in Cr₂O₃, acts as a diffusion barrier for underlying metallic constituents, while the presence of ZrO₂ and HfO₂ precipitates within the bulk contributes to a mixed‑phase protective network that reduces oxygen permeation. The alloy demonstrates superior oxidation resistance compared to binary refractory counterparts, attributable to synergistic lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening, which suppress grain boundary diffusion and mitigate scale spallation. These findings suggest that the engineered microstructural features inherent to CrHfWReNbZrTi enhance its high‑temperature oxidative stability, rendering it a promising candidate for structural applications in oxidizing environments.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: Arc melting of the equiatomic mixtures ZrReHfWTi and NbCrTaTiHf was followed by rapid drop casting to produce cast ingots with minimal cooling gradients. Post‑solidification, specimens were machined into notched dog‑bone coupons, with notch radii of 0.5 mm, and subjected to monotonic tensile loading to failure. The BCC framework of both alloys, coupled with high lattice distortion, promotes a high density of twin boundaries that act as barriers to crack propagation. However, the ZrReHfWTi composition incorporates Zr and Ti, which tend to stabilize a more ductile microstructure and increase the propensity for microcrack deflection, thereby reducing notch sensitivity and yielding comparatively higher fracture toughness. In contrast, NbCrTaTiHf contains a higher fraction of Cr and Nb, elements that favor the formation of fine, coherent precipitates that can act as crack initiators, raising notch sensitivity and diminishing fracture toughness. Consequently, the ZrReHfWTi alloy is expected to exhibit a lower notch effect and better fracture resistance than NbCrTaTiHf.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: The vacuum‑induction melted WTaNb alloy, possessing a nearly equiatomic composition, displayed a moderate increase in elongation at fracture relative to its binary counterparts, as inferred from compact‑tension fracture toughness specimens. Fine, equiaxed grains resulting from rapid solidification were observed, and their uniform distribution contributed to a more homogeneous stress field during crack propagation, thereby delaying the onset of micro‑void coalescence. However, the high lattice distortion inherent to the refractory elements produced localized stress concentrators that facilitated the initiation of shear bands at lower applied strains. The presence of minor amorphous intergranular phases, likely formed during cooling, acted as crack‑bridging entities, enhancing energy absorption and permitting additional plastic strain before catastrophic failure. Nonetheless, the relatively coarse precipitates of Ta–W rich intermetallics occasionally served as crack initiation sites, limiting the ultimate ductility. Overall, the interplay between fine grains, lattice distortion, and intergranular features governs the observed balance between elongation at fracture and fracture toughness in this system.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy NbVWReZrHf, fabricated by arc melting and subsequent drop casting, was evaluated for high‑temperature performance relative to conventional Ni‑based superalloys. The multi‑principal composition generates a significant lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation glide and yields a markedly higher yield strength at temperatures above 900 °C compared with Ni‑based alloys that rely primarily on γ′ precipitation for strength. The fine, homogenous microstructure of the drop‑cast material, with grain sizes below 30 µm, reduces the likelihood of creep‑driven grain boundary sliding, leading to a superior creep resistance that remains stable up to 1100 °C. Moreover, the absence of detrimental intermetallic formation and the inherent stability of the body‑centered cubic phase in NbVWReZrHf prevent the loss of strength often observed in Ni‑based superalloys under prolonged thermal exposure. Consequently, this HEA exhibits a more favorable combination of high‑temperature yield strength, elastic modulus, and fracture toughness than its Ni‑based counterparts, positioning it as a promising candidate for next‑generation turbine and power‑generation components.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: Arc‑melting of equiatomic NbTiMo and VTaReZrMoTi powders was conducted under high‑purity argon, followed by rapid cooling through drop casting into a copper mold to promote a fine equiaxed microstructure. In the NbTiMo alloy, the close atomic size match between Nb, Ti, and Mo yields a nearly lattice‑coherent solid solution, with negligible secondary phase formation. This homogenization, together with a fine grain size (≈10 µm) observed by SEM, facilitates dislocation glide and a relatively high elongation at fracture. By contrast, the VTaReZrMoTi system exhibits pronounced lattice distortion due to the larger size difference between Re and the other elements, leading to the nucleation of small, incoherent intermetallic precipitates during solidification. These precipitates, spaced roughly 200 nm apart, act as obstacles to dislocation motion and serve as sites for stress concentration, thereby reducing ductility. Consequently, the NbTiMo alloy would be expected to display a higher elongation at fracture than VTaReZrMoTi, driven by its more coherent solid solution and finer, less heterogeneous microstructure.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory BCC high‑entropy alloys MoNbHfWCr and TaTiHf under a controlled argon atmosphere produced dense, near‑equimolar microstructures, yet distinct differences in notch sensitivity emerge from their compositional and structural attributes. In MoNbHfWCr the higher concentration of transition metals with substantial atomic size mismatch induces pronounced lattice distortion, enhancing solid‑solution hardening while simultaneously promoting a finer, more uniform grain network. This grain refinement reduces the likelihood of crack initiation at notches, thereby elevating the fracture toughness relative to the TaTiHf counterpart. Conversely, TaTiHf contains a greater proportion of large‑size elements that tend to form coarse, intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries; these secondary phases act as stress concentrators and facilitate crack propagation from notches, increasing notch sensitivity. Consequently, the MoNbHfWCr alloy would plausibly exhibit lower notch sensitivity and higher fracture toughness, whereas TaTiHf would trend toward greater notch sensitivity and reduced toughness in their brittle BCC compositions.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy VReNbZrTiCr by directed energy deposition yields a complex, multiphase microstructure in which rapid solidification and directional cooling produce pronounced dendritic segregation. Columnar dendrites form along the build direction, with primary arms enriched in high‑melting‑point constituents such as V and Nb, while secondary arms incorporate more refractory Re and Zr. This chemical inhomogeneity generates compositional gradients that are reflected in locally varying lattice parameters and solid solution strengthening. The overall grain size is markedly refined relative to conventional casting, with equiaxed grains of a few hundred micrometers appearing in the interdendritic regions where the local composition is more homogeneous. The combination of dendritic segregation and fine, directionally biased grains enhances resistance to crack initiation, while the presence of minor secondary phases at grain boundaries can impede dislocation motion, contributing to elevated yield strength and hardness in the as‑printed state.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: Powder metallurgy was employed to fabricate bulk TiZrHf specimens, with elemental powders mixed at an equiatomic ratio and milled under argon to promote intimate contact and reduce contamination. The blended powders were compacted to 70 % theoretical density and then subjected to spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1900 °C under a uniaxial pressure of 50 MPa for 5 min, using a heating rate of 100 °C min⁻¹. The rapid heating and short dwell time minimized grain growth, yielding a fine‑grained, nearly single‑phase solid solution dominated by a bcc matrix. During fatigue testing in a closed‑loop servo‑hydraulic machine at room temperature, initial crack nucleation was observed predominantly at grain boundary–phase interfaces, suggesting that local lattice distortion and residual stresses concentrated there. As loading cycles increased, cracks propagated along the plane of maximum shear, with intermittent slowing at high‑angle grain boundaries that acted as barrier sites. The overall fatigue life correlated positively with the fine grain size and the absence of large porosity, while any secondary precipitates or retained oxides accelerated crack growth by serving as stress concentrators.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Suction casting of the refractory high entropy alloy VWZr was conducted in a sealed quartz tube under a continuous flow of high‑purity argon to suppress oxidation of the molten alloy, which possesses a nominal composition of V_25W_25Zr_25Cu_25 (percent by weight). The melt, maintained at 2600 °C, was rapidly drawn through a 1.5 mm diameter nozzle, producing a dense column that was immediately quenched in a liquid nitrogen bath to lock in the high‑temperature solid solution structure and minimize grain growth. Post‑solidification, the surface of the cast rod was subjected to a two‑step coating protocol: first, a thin (≈2 µm) TiN layer was deposited by magnetron sputtering under 5 mTorr nitrogen at 550 °C, providing a barrier to high‑temperature oxidation and enhancing surface hardness; second, a conformal Al₂O₃ film was applied via atomic layer deposition at 300 °C to improve thermal shock resistance. Microstructural analysis revealed that the TiN/Al₂O₃ bilayer adheres to the VWZr matrix through interfacial diffusion of Ti and Al, forming a graded interface that mitigates thermal mismatch stresses during temperature cycling. The coated samples exhibited markedly reduced oxidation rates when exposed to 1200 °C in air, as evidenced by weight‑gain measurements and X‑ray diffraction that showed only minor formation of V₂O₅ and W₃O₈, confirming the efficacy of the dual‑layer strategy for high‑temperature surface protection.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: high-temperature coating or surface protection strategies
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: CrWTa and CrTaTi were synthesized from elemental powders using spark plasma sintering, yielding dense microstructures with similar overall porosity. In both systems the dominant phase is a body‑centered cubic (BCC) matrix, yet CrWTa contains a minor intermetallic TiC‑rich secondary phase that segregates to grain boundaries, whereas CrTaTi exhibits a homogeneous solid solution with only trace amounts of TiC. The TiC precipitates in CrWTa increase local stress concentrations and promote transgranular fracture, reducing the ease with which a crack can be deflected along grain boundaries. Conversely, the absence of pronounced secondary phases in CrTaTi allows for more effective grain‑boundary sliding and the formation of tortuous crack paths, which enhances fracture resistance. Accordingly, CrTaTi is expected to display superior fracture toughness relative to CrWTa, driven by its cleaner grain‑boundary chemistry and higher propensity for crack‑path deflection.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fracture toughness trends and their relation to phase content, grain boundary character, and crack path

text: Arc‑melted ingots of the refractory HEA ZrHfReCr were repeatedly melted under an argon atmosphere, then drop‑cast into copper molds to promote rapid solidification. Microstructural examination revealed a homogeneous BCC matrix interspersed with nanoscale Laves‑type Zr₂Cr and HfRe precipitates that increased in volume fraction as the Zr:Hf ratio was elevated. Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy (RUS) measured a monotonic rise in the longitudinal elastic modulus with decreasing Zr content, attributable to the higher lattice stiffness of the Re–rich matrix. Hardness mapping showed that specimens with intermediate Zr levels exhibited the greatest microhardness, correlating with an optimal balance between solid‑solution strengthening from the alloying elements and fine precipitate spacing that impedes dislocation motion. In contrast, Zr‑rich compositions, while retaining higher elastic modulus, displayed lower hardness due to coarser precipitates and a reduced degree of lattice distortion. These observations underscore the critical role of secondary phase content and compositional tuning in tailoring the mechanical performance of ZrHfReCr.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Arc‑melting of a stoichiometric TaMoWVZrTi batch was performed under a high‑purity argon atmosphere with a 50 mm water‑cooled copper crucible, ensuring complete homogenization of the refractory elements and minimizing vaporization losses. The resulting ingot was subsequently drop‑cast onto a graphite mold to produce a dense, near‑single‑phase cast alloy. Optical microscopy revealed a lamellar microstructure composed of fine equiaxed grains (average size < 5 µm) interspersed with weakly coherent intermetallic precipitates enriched in W and V. Scanning electron microscopy of fatigue specimens showed crack initiation preferentially at grain boundary junctions where localized stress concentrations are highest; the presence of the secondary W‑rich phases acted to blunt the crack tip, slowing early propagation. Electron backscatter diffraction mapped the lattice distortion around the precipitates, confirming a high degree of solid‑solution strengthening that contributed to a higher threshold stress intensity for crack advance. Moreover, the negligible porosity observed in the as‑cast microstructure reduced extrinsic fatigue damage, leading to a longer fatigue life compared to wrought counterparts with higher defect densities.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Processing the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaHfVMo by vacuum induction melting yields a single‑phase body‑centered cubic microstructure with modest grain refinement. Instrumented indentation tests on this material reveal a pronounced hardness increase relative to its constituent binary alloys, indicating significant solid‑solution strengthening from the large lattice distortion introduced by the disparate atomic radii of Ta, Hf, V, and Mo. However, the same microstructural features that raise hardness also impede dislocation mobility, leading to a reduced elastic modulus as measured by the slope of the unloading curve. This stiffening manifests as a limited capacity for plastic deformation, evidenced by low load‑deformation curves and a narrow plastic region during indentation. Consequently, the alloy displays a classic ductility‑strength trade‑off: as hardness and elastic modulus rise due to the high lattice distortion and potential short‑range ordering, the material’s ability to undergo significant elongation before fracture diminishes, underscoring the need to balance grain size and compositional tuning to optimize both strength and ductility.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)
style: a textbook passage explaining the concept to a graduate student

text: Arc‐melting and drop casting produce dense ingots of the refractory high‑entropy alloys NbReWVMoHf and TiWCr, yet their microstructural evolution leads to distinct ductility–strength balances. In NbReWVMoHf, the near‑equimolar combination of large‑size elements (Nb, W, Hf) with smaller Mo and V generates significant lattice distortion and a fine, homogeneous γ‑phase that promotes solid‑solution hardening. The resulting high yield and ultimate tensile strengths are offset by limited slip system activation, yielding reduced elongation to failure. Conversely, TiWCr, containing the smaller Ti atom and a higher proportion of Cr, exhibits a more relaxed lattice parameter mismatch and a dual‑phase microstructure where a minor TiC precipitate is interspersed within a BCC matrix. This arrangement provides moderate strengthening while maintaining a higher number of available slip systems, thereby enhancing ductility relative to NbReWVMoHf. Consequently, TiWCr is expected to show a more favorable strength–ductility trade‑off, achieving comparable strength with greater elongation to fracture.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: In suction casting of TiCrZrTaMo and CrZrTaTiMoReV alloys under argon, microstructural examination revealed contrasting hardness trends attributable to secondary phase chemistry and distribution. The TiCrZrTaMo cast exhibited a largely single BCC solid solution with occasional Ti-rich precipitates, producing a relatively uniform hardness profile and modestly higher hardness relative to the CrZrTaTiMoReV alloy. By contrast, CrZrTaTiMoReV developed a fine network of intermetallic Ti₂Zr and Re-containing intergranular phases that fragmented the microstructure; the presence of these hard, but brittle intermetallics tended to increase peak hardness locally while also inducing porosity at grain boundaries, which in turn lowered overall hardness. Thus, the TiCrZrTaMo alloy is expected to trend higher in bulk hardness due to its simpler phase constitution and lower porosity, whereas CrZrTaTiMoReV shows a broader hardness distribution driven by secondary phase content and intergranular porosity.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: ZrNbTaMo ingots were fabricated by vacuum induction melting with an arc power of 2.5 kW and a melt duration of 15 s per pass, repeated four times to ensure homogeneity. After casting, the ingots were hot‐rolled at 1400 °C to 30 % reduction, followed by solution annealing at 1550 °C for 2 h under argon. Recrystallization was monitored by in situ synchrotron X‑ray diffraction, revealing a shift of the (110) reflection from a broad, heavily strained state to a sharp peak indicative of complete strain relief at 1450 °C. Electron backscatter diffraction maps showed nucleation of equiaxed grains at about 1300 °C, with grain size increasing from an initial 5 µm to ~30 µm by 1500 °C. Grain growth followed a power‑law kinetics (D² ∝ t) with a growth exponent of 0.6, suggesting that lattice distortion and limited diffusion of Zr in the high‑entropy matrix retard growth relative to conventional refractory alloys. The resulting microstructure exhibited a uniform grain distribution and low porosity, which are expected to influence the alloy’s high‑temperature mechanical performance.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering produced a dense VTaReHfWCr alloy whose microstructure is dominated by a fine network of secondary precipitates. During the rapid sintering step the high solute concentration and substantial lattice distortion of the solid solution drive the precipitation of Laves‑type phases, notably (V,Cr)₂W and (Ta,Re)Hf₂, which nucleate heterogeneously at grain boundaries and along dislocation cores. The Laves phases form at relatively low volume fractions yet create a highly non‑equiaxed morphology that impedes dislocation motion through Orowan bowing. Concurrently, minor intermetallics such as Ta₃Cr and V₆Hf precipitate as coherent islands within the matrix, contributing additional solid‑solution and precipitation hardening. The combined effect of these second phases is a substantial increase in yield strength and hardness while the grain boundary network retains sufficient ductility, as the fine precipitates act as obstacles without severely compromising strain‑tolerance. The resulting microstructure thus balances strength and toughness through controlled secondary phase precipitation.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: secondary phase precipitation (Laves phases, intermetallics)

text: Suction casting of WZrCr and ZrNbMoV was carried out in a quartz crucible under an argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation. Both alloys were cast at 1700 °C and immediately quenched in liquid nitrogen, producing a fine-grained microstructure with a near-equiatomic lattice and limited secondary phase formation. Electron backscatter diffraction revealed that the WZrCr matrix exhibits a higher lattice distortion due to the larger atomic size mismatch between W and Cr, while the ZrNbMoV alloy shows a more homogeneous solid solution with a lower overall strain field. Hardness measurements performed on polished cross‑sections indicated that WZrCr is consistently harder than ZrNbMoV, which is consistent with the Tabor relation linking hardness to yield strength: the greater lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening in WZrCr should translate into a higher yield stress. Accordingly, tensile tests displayed a higher yield point for WZrCr, corroborating the hardness trend and suggesting that the increased resistance to dislocation motion in the W‑rich matrix dominates the mechanical response.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)
style: an experimental methods and observations section

text: Laser additive manufacturing via directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate cylindrical test specimens of two refractory high‑entropy alloys: TaCrReHfMoW (Ta‑Cr‑Re‑Hf‑Mo‑W) and TiWHfZrTaMo (Ti‑W‑Hf‑Zr‑Ta‑Mo). Process parameters were matched to yield comparable melt‑pool geometries and minimal macro‑porosity, but the TiWHfZrTaMo build exhibited a higher degree of columnar grain growth along the deposition direction due to the larger lattice mismatch among Ti, W, and Hf. In high‑cycle fatigue tests at room temperature, crack initiation in TaCrReHfMoW preferentially occurred at sites of residual compressive stress accumulation associated with finer equiaxed grains and a more homogeneous distribution of solid solution strengthening, leading to a slower propagation rate governed by frequent micro‑crack deflection. Conversely, TiWHfZrTaMo showed early initiation along the columnar grain boundaries where the Ti–W–Hf network facilitates localized slip and a higher propensity for micro‑void coalescence. Consequently, the fatigue life of TaCrReHfMoW is plausibly higher than that of TiWHfZrTaMo, driven by its finer grain structure, lower porosity, and more uniform solid‑solution strengthening field that impede crack nucleation and reduce the effective crack‑growth velocity.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
